items.ms: (a) Unpolarised has oscillations in many directions/planes (1); polarised has oscillations in a single direction/plane (1); perpendicular to (or including) the direction of energy transfer (1). (b) Photograph B: reflected light is partially polarised (1), perpendicular to the filter's plane so blocked/absorbed (1, 1).
path: Waves and Particle Nature of Light
S49 - what is meant by plane polarisation

items.name: Slinky spring longitudinal wave description
items.how: Describe the waves demonstrated by a slinky spring driven by a hand oscillating left to right.
items.ms: Longitudinal wave (1); compressions and rarefactions (1); oscillations parallel to direction of wave travel (1); one extra detail such as progressive wave, example (sound), pressure variation or wavelength between adjacent compressions (1).
path: Waves and Particle Nature of Light
S35 - describe longitudinal waves in terms of press

items.name: Radio reception behind hill by diffraction
items.how: Explain how 693 kHz broadcasts can be received on the far side of a hill, including an appropriate calculation.
items.ms: Mention diffraction (1); wavelength comparable to or greater than the hill's size (1); use v = f lambda with 3e8 m/s (1); lambda = 433 m (1).
path: Waves and Particle Nature of Light
S50 - what is meant by diffraction and use Huygens

items.name: Radio wave energy reaching head
items.how: Calculate the energy arriving at a person's head in one hour from radio waves of given radiation flux and head area.
items.ms: Flux = power per unit area, so power = flux x area (1); energy = power x time (1); E = 7.5e-7 J (1).
path: Waves and Particle Nature of Light
S44 - use the equation for the intensity of radiati

items.name: Meaning of 180 degree phase difference
items.how: Explain what is meant by a phase difference of 180 degrees.
items.ms: Waves are in antiphase (half a cycle out of phase, or path difference of lambda/2) (1); they would destructively interfere (1).
path: Waves and Particle Nature of Light
S39 - what is meant by wavefront, coherence, path d

items.name: Speed of light in oil
items.how: Calculate the velocity of light in oil of refractive index 1.5. The input shows only part (b)(i).
items.ms: Use n = c/v with c = 3.0e8 m/s (1); v = 2.0e8 m/s (1). MS also has (b)(ii) for 5 marks, a QWC thin-film constructive interference argument (not shown in input).
path: Waves and Particle Nature of Light
S45 - that at the interface between medium 1 and me

items.name: Explaining the photoelectric effect
items.how: Explain the photoelectric effect.
items.ms: Photons are absorbed and transfer energy to electrons (1); electrons are released when the photon energy exceeds the work function (1).

S59 - that the absorption of a photon can result in

items.name: Planck constant from photoelectric graph
items.how: Use a graph of maximum kinetic energy against frequency to determine the Planck constant. The input shows only part (b)(i).
items.ms: Calculate the gradient using at least half the graph (1); h = 6.3e-34 J s, range 6.2e-34 to 6.4e-34 (1). MS also has (b)(ii) threshold frequency (2) and (b)(iii) work function 1.5-1.7 eV (3), not shown in input.
path: Waves and Particle Nature of Light
S60 - the terms threshold frequency and work functi

items.name: Resistivity of ground between electrodes
items.how: Calculate the resistivity of the ground from a 12 V supply, 8.5 mA current, 0.80 m electrode spacing and 0.25 m^2 effective area.
items.ms: Use V = IR (1); use R = rho l / A (1); rho = 440 ohm m (1).
path: S71 - use the equation R  A

items.name: Ground layers matched to resistivity graph
items.how: Explain how a sketch of top soil, wet subsoil and bedrock corresponds to a graph of resistivity against depth.
items.ms: State a resistivity value for a layer (1); compare resistivities between layers (1); interpret the shape, e.g. gradual decrease from topsoil to subsoil shows a varying depth or incline, sudden increase at 5 m shows bedrock (1).
path: S71 - use the equation R  A

items.name: Voltmeter reading with four electrodes
items.how: Explain the voltmeter reading expected across two inner electrodes 0.20 m apart when the cross-sectional area is constant. The input shows only part (c)(i).
items.ms: Potential-divider reasoning: resistance is proportional to length (1), so V is proportional to l (1); V = 3 V (12 V x 0.20/0.80) (1). MS also has (c)(ii) for 1 mark (not shown in input).

deps.name: Resistivity of ground between electrodes

path: S74 - how the potential along a uniform current-car

items.name: Lamp brightness when switch closed
items.how: Multi-part; the input shows only (a): three identical 1.5 V lamps with two cells, explain the change in brightness of each lamp when the switch is closed (6 marks). The mark scheme also covers (b), the I-V characteristic of a filament lamp.
items.ms: (a) B brighter, A dimmer (1); resistance of the parallel combination and circuit decreases (1); circuit current increases (1); p.d. across B increases, across A (and C) decreases (1); current shared equally between A and C (1); A and C same brightness (1). (b)(i) symmetrical I-V curve through the origin (2); (b)(ii) resistance rises with temperature through more lattice vibrations and collisions (4).
path: S68 - derive the equations for combining resistance

items.name: SI unit of density
items.how: Multiple choice: choose the SI unit for density.
items.ms: D (kg m^-3).

items.name: Mean reaction time with uncertainty
items.how: Multiple choice: from four reaction-time readings (one anomalous), choose the best mean with a suitable uncertainty.
items.ms: B (0.20 +/- 0.01 s): discard the anomalous 0.09 s, mean of the other three, uncertainty from the spread.

items.name: Quantity not needed for viscous drag
items.how: Multiple choice: in finding viscous drag on a sphere falling at constant speed, choose the quantity not required.
items.ms: C (mass of sphere): Stokes' law F = 6 pi eta r v needs the diameter and the speed (from height and time), not the mass.

items.name: Spring constant from extension-force graph
items.how: Multiple choice: from a graph of extension against force, choose how the force constant k is found.
items.ms: D (the inverse of the gradient), since the axes are extension (y) and force (x).

items.name: Spring energy from graph area
items.how: Multiple choice: choose how to find the energy stored when the spring is stretched by 6 cm, using the same graph.
items.ms: B (the area under the graph), as given by the mark scheme.

deps.name: Spring constant from extension-force graph

items.name: Voltmeter needs very high resistance
items.how: Explain why the voltmeter in a circuit measuring a wire's resistance should have a very high resistance.
items.ms: Voltmeter is in parallel with the wire (1); it should draw negligible current (1); so the ammeter reading is the current in the wire and R = V/I is correct (1); link between voltmeter resistance and the calculated resistance (max 3).

items.name: Purpose of variable resistor
items.how: Explain why a variable resistor is included in the circuit for finding a wire's resistance.
items.ms: To limit/vary/control the current so the wire's temperature and resistance do not change (1), and to give a range of readings for plotting a graph (1).

items.name: Stair power: apparatus list
items.how: Plan part (a): list the apparatus needed to find the power of a student running up stairs.
items.ms: Timing mechanism (stopwatch or light gates with datalogger), rule/tape, balance/scales (1).

items.name: Stair power: quantities to measure
items.how: Plan part (b): state the quantities to be measured.
items.ms: Mass (or weight), height (vertical distance) and time (1).

items.name: Stair power: choice of instruments
items.how: Plan part (c): for two of the quantities, explain the choice of measuring instrument.
items.ms: Max 2 per quantity: instrument named plus justification, e.g. balance with a scale suited to the expected mass; metre rule with 1 mm divisions and adequate range; stopwatch reading to 0.1 s with reference to reaction time or percentage uncertainty.

deps.name: Stair power: quantities to measure

items.name: Stair power: repeat readings
items.how: Plan part (d): comment on whether repeat readings are appropriate.
items.ms: Max 2: the student may tire so speed/power changes; repeat after rest; repeat the height measurement; difficulty of starting and stopping the timing.

items.name: Stair power: calculating power from data
items.how: Plan part (e): explain how the data collected will be used to determine the power.
items.ms: Explain how total height is found (vertical distance) (1); use mgh or force x distance (1); power equation, e.g. P = mgh/t (1).

deps.name: Stair power: quantities to measure

items.name: Stair power: uncertainty and systematic error
items.how: Plan part (f): identify the main sources of uncertainty and/or systematic error.
items.ms: Max 2 from: reaction time, different starting/stopping points, parallax, zero errors.

items.name: Stair power: safety comment
items.how: Plan part (g): comment on safety.
items.ms: A relevant hazard with a precaution, e.g. collisions on the stairs (keep them clear), suitable footwear against falls, knee pads/headwear (1).

items.name: Accurate ray measurements for refraction
items.how: Suggest what the student should do to make measurements of angles of incidence and refraction as accurate as possible with a semicircular block.
items.ms: Max 2 from: trace the ray with paper and pins; use a thin ray; aim at the centre of the block; draw the normal at A and measure from it; mark the ray then measure the angle; use a wide range of large angles; repeat and average; work in a dark room.

items.name: Criticise refraction results table
items.how: Criticise the student's table of angles of incidence and refraction.
items.ms: Max 3 from: missing unit; too few results; no repeats or mean; inconsistent increase in angle or a large gap between the first two readings; small range; inconsistent precision of i and r.

items.name: Draw normal, measure angles, find sines
items.how: On a diagram, draw a normal at A, measure i and r for the last row, and complete the sin i and sin r values in the table.
items.ms: Normal correctly drawn with a rule (1); i = 40 +/- 1 degrees (1); r = 25 +/- 1 degrees (1); correct sines to 3 s.f. for their angles (1).

items.name: Plot sin i against sin r + Refractive index from graph gradient
items.how: Use the graph to determine a value for the refractive index mu.
items.ms: mu = gradient of the graph (1); substitute pairs of readings from a large triangle on their line (1); mu between 1.45 and 1.60, 2 or 3 s.f., no unit (1).

items.name: Correct unit for stress
items.how: Multiple choice: choose the correct unit for stress.
items.ms: D (Pa).

items.name: Quantity with no unit
items.how: Multiple choice: choose the quantity that does not have a unit.
items.ms: C (strain, a ratio of lengths).

items.name: Mean fall time excluding anomaly
items.how: Multiple choice: four stopwatch times for a dropped tennis ball, one anomalous; choose the mean to record.
items.ms: B (0.77 s): disregard the anomalous 0.97 s, average the rest, and quote to the precision of the data.

items.name: Equation to calculate g directly
items.how: Multiple choice: for a ball dropped from rest through a measured height, choose the equation that gives g directly.
items.ms: B (s = ut + 1/2 at^2): with u = 0, s and t give a = g directly.

deps.name: Mean fall time excluding anomaly

items.name: Liquid density unit conversion
items.how: Multiple choice: convert 100 g in 80 cm^3 to a density in kg m^-3.

items.name: Young modulus wire risk assessment table
items.how: Complete a partly filled risk-assessment table (apparatus, hazard, risk, precaution) for a Young modulus experiment with a wire and hanging weights.
items.ms: Wire: hazard (snaps) with specific risk (eye injury) and precaution (goggles) (1 + 1); hanging weights: hazard (fall) with specific risk (foot injury) (1) and precaution (keep feet clear, sand box, protective shoes) (1). Must be specific injuries and precautions.

items.name: Bulb resistance: circuit diagram
items.how: Plan part (a): draw the circuit to investigate how the resistance of a 12 V, 24 W bulb varies with p.d.
items.ms: Correct circuit with ammeter, voltmeter, power supply and bulb (1); variable resistor, potential divider or variable supply (1).

items.name: Bulb resistance: quantities to measure
items.how: Plan part (b): state the quantities to be measured.
items.ms: Potential difference and current (1).

items.name: Bulb resistance: measuring instrument choice
items.how: Plan part (c): explain the choice of measuring instrument for two of the quantities.
items.ms: Voltmeter or multimeter set on an identified range of at least 12 V (2); ammeter/multimeter set on an identified range of at least 2 A (2).

deps.name: Bulb resistance: quantities to measure

items.name: Bulb resistance: repeat readings
items.how: Plan part (d): comment on whether repeat readings are appropriate.
items.ms: An appropriate comment with justification, e.g. no, as the bulb gets hot; or yes, repeat after the bulb has cooled (1).

items.name: Bulb resistance: analysis and sketch graph
items.how: Plan part (e): explain how the data will be used and sketch the expected graph.
items.ms: Determine R from V and I (1); plot R against V (1); sketch showing R increasing with V with a positive intercept on the R axis (1).

deps.name: Bulb resistance: quantities to measure

items.name: Bulb resistance: uncertainty sources
items.how: Plan part (f): identify the main sources of uncertainty and/or systematic error.
items.ms: Zero error on an analogue meter, or difficulty taking simultaneous measurements (1).

items.name: Bulb resistance: safety comment
items.how: Plan part (g): comment on safety.
items.ms: Low-voltage supply so low risk, or the bulb gets hot so do not touch it (1).

items.name: Missing r squared value and unit
items.how: Complete the table of r, r^2 and terminal velocity v with the missing r^2 value and its unit.
items.ms: 9 mm^2 (or 9e-6 m^2), with r^2 values 1, 4, 9, 16 mm^2 (1).

items.name: Criticise glycerol viscosity results
items.how: Criticise the results table of sphere radius and terminal velocity.
items.ms: Max 2 from: too few results; small range; no repeats or means; lack of precision in radius; inconsistent s.f. in v.

items.name: Why v against r squared is linear
items.how: Explain why v against r^2 should be a straight line with gradient 2g(rho_s - rho_g)/9 eta.
items.ms: Compare explicitly or implicitly with y = mx (1); the gradient factor is constant because g, rho_s, rho_g and eta are constant (dependent mark) (1).

items.name: Factors affecting measured viscosity
items.how: Suggest two factors in the experiment that would affect the value of eta.
items.ms: Max 2 from: terminal velocity not reached; temperature not constant; spheres thrown rather than dropped; accuracy of manufacturer's radius or diameter. Other sensible physics accepted.

items.name: Plot v against r squared + Gradient of v against r squared graph
items.how: Use the graph to determine a value for the gradient.
items.ms: Triangle using more than half the drawn line (1); points read correctly from the line (1); gradient calculated to at least 2 s.f. (1).

items.name: Plot v against r squared + Gradient of v against r squared graph + Viscosity of glycerol from gradient
items.how: Use the gradient to calculate the viscosity eta, given the steel and glycerol densities.
items.ms: Substitute into gradient = 2g(rho_s - rho_g)/9 eta (1); eta in the range 1.45-1.70 (1); 2 or 3 s.f. with unit (Pa s) (1). Example 1.6 Pa s.

items.name: Base SI unit identification
items.how: Multiple choice: choose the base SI unit from ampere, newton, pascal and watt.
items.ms: A (ampere); the others are derived units.

items.name: Micrometer screw gauge reading
items.how: Multiple choice: read a micrometer screw gauge diagram, in mm.

items.name: V against I relationship for cell
items.how: Multiple choice: for a V against I graph from a variable-resistor circuit with a cell, choose the correct description of the relationship.
items.ms: C: there is a linear relationship (a negative-gradient straight line with a non-zero intercept, so not directly proportional).

items.name: E.m.f. from graph intercept
items.how: Multiple choice: from the V against I graph, choose which feature gives the cell's e.m.f.
items.ms: D: the intercept on the V axis.

deps.name: V against I relationship for cell

items.name: Gradient magnitude of V-I graph
items.how: Multiple choice: choose the magnitude of the gradient of the V against I graph.
items.ms: B (1.96), the internal resistance in ohm.

deps.name: V against I relationship for cell

items.name: Range of density measurements
items.how: State the range of measurements for a density quoted as 8700 +/- 200 kg m^-3.
items.ms: 8500 to 8900 kg m^-3 (a range of 400 kg m^-3 also accepted) (1).

items.name: Percentage uncertainty in density
items.how: Calculate the percentage uncertainty in a density of 8700 +/- 200 kg m^-3.

items.name: Identify metal from density range
items.how: Using a table of densities for brass, bronze and copper, state which metal the student used.
items.ms: Bronze (8810 kg m^-3 lies within 8500-8900), or a choice consistent with their value (1).

deps.name: Range of density measurements

items.name: Motor efficiency: quantities to measure
items.how: Plan part (a): state the quantities to be measured to find the efficiency of a 9 V motor lifting a 1 kg mass at steady speed.
items.ms: Potential difference, current, height and time: 1 mark for two correct quantities, 2 marks for all four; no credit for mass/weight.

items.name: Motor efficiency: choice of instruments
items.how: Plan part (b): explain the choice of measuring instrument for two of the quantities.
items.ms: Max 2 per quantity: instrument plus justification, e.g. metre rule with 1 mm divisions for height; voltmeter with 0.1 V precision or 0-15 V range for a 9 V battery.

deps.name: Motor efficiency: quantities to measure

items.name: Motor efficiency: repeat readings
items.how: Plan part (c): comment on whether repeat readings are appropriate.
items.ms: Yes, to average for reliability; or no, as the motor heats up or the battery p.d. falls (1).

items.name: Motor efficiency: calculating from data
items.how: Plan part (d): explain how the data will be used to calculate the efficiency of the motor.
items.ms: Power in = VI and power out = mgh/t (or energy in = VIt, energy out = mgh) (2); efficiency = output/input (1); an explicit graphical method (h against t gradient x mg/VI) is also accepted.

deps.name: Motor efficiency: quantities to measure

items.name: Motor efficiency: uncertainty and systematic error
items.how: Plan part (e): identify the main sources of uncertainty and/or systematic error.
items.ms: Max 2 from: parallax/random error in a named measurement; zero error in a named instrument; string slipping on the winding mechanism; reaction time.

items.name: Motor efficiency: safety comment
items.how: Plan part (f): comment on safety.
items.ms: Identify a risk with a precaution, e.g. mass falling on feet (wear shoes), eye injury if the string breaks (goggles), or low risk as only 9 V (1).

items.name: Criticise rubber stretching results
items.how: Criticise the table of extension and force for a rubber strip.
items.ms: Max 2 from: inconsistent s.f./precision in extension; no repeats; length of rubber not measured to nearest mm. Small range and inconsistent intervals are not credited.

items.name: Plot and describe rubber force-extension graph
items.how: (i) Plot force (y) against extension (x) and draw a line of best fit (4 marks); (ii) comment on the shape of the graph (2 marks). The mark scheme also has a (b)(iii) worth 4 marks, work done from the area under the graph, which is not in the input.
items.ms: (i) Sensible scales (1); plotting all correct (2, or 1 for one error) (2); smooth curve through all points (1). (ii) Non-linear/changing gradient, does not obey Hooke's law, initially hard to stretch then easier or harder as it lengthens, identify linear sections (max 2). (iii) area gives about 1.6-1.75 J (4).

items.name: Stress and strain of rubber, assumption
items.how: For the last row of the results, calculate the stress and strain and state an assumption made.
items.ms: Stress = F/A with A = 1.05e-3 x 2.71e-3 m^2 (2.85e-6 m^2) (2), stress = 6.5e6 Pa (1); strain = extension/original length (1), strain = 2.3 with no unit (1); assumption that the cross-section stays constant (1).

items.name: SI base unit identification
items.how: Multiple choice: which of force, newton, second, time is an SI base unit.
items.ms: C (second). Newton is a derived unit; force and time are quantities, not units.

items.name: Mean time with uncertainty, anomaly
items.how: Multiple choice: choose the mean and uncertainty for four timings, one of which (0.59 s) is anomalous.
items.ms: B (0.70 +/- 0.01 s): anomalous reading omitted, then mean 0.70 s with half-range uncertainty. A has the wrong uncertainty; C and D keep the anomaly.

items.name: Young modulus: quantity not needed
items.how: Multiple choice on a Young modulus wire experiment: which of density, extension, force, original length is not needed.
items.ms: A (density). Extension, force applied and original length all appear in the required relationship.

items.name: Instrument for wire diameter
items.how: Multiple choice: which instrument should measure the diameter of the wire in the Young modulus experiment (stem given in Q3).
items.ms: C (micrometer screw gauge), which has sufficient precision for a wire diameter; rules and vernier callipers do not.

deps.name: Young modulus: quantity not needed

items.name: SI unit of Young modulus
items.how: Multiple choice: which is a correct unit for the Young modulus (N, N m^-1, Pa, Pa m^-1); context given in Q3.
items.ms: C (Pa). The other options are not accepted SI units for the Young modulus.

deps.name: Young modulus: quantity not needed

items.name: Speed of sound: procedure outline
items.how: Plan question (speed of sound with two microphones and a dual-beam oscilloscope): outline the experimental procedure.
items.ms: Marked holistically, 1 mark each: separate the microphones; measure the distance between them; measure the time difference; between the peaks on the two oscilloscope traces.

items.name: Speed of sound: additional apparatus
items.how: List any additional apparatus needed beyond the microphones and oscilloscope shown.
items.ms: 1 mark for a metre rule or tape measure; 1 mark for a means of making a short sound.

items.name: Speed of sound: variables to measure
items.how: State the quantities to be measured and identify the independent and dependent variables.
items.ms: 1 mark for distance and time; 1 mark for distance as the independent variable and time as the dependent variable.

items.name: Speed of sound: repeat readings
items.how: Comment on whether repeat readings are appropriate.
items.ms: Yes: so a mean can be calculated (1) and to reduce random errors or anomalous results (1).

items.name: Speed of sound: using data v=s/t
items.how: State how the data collected will be used to determine the speed of sound.
items.ms: 1 mark for use of v = s/t.

deps.name: Speed of sound: variables to measure

items.name: Speed of sound: uncertainty and systematic error
items.how: Identify the main sources of uncertainty and/or systematic error and explain how to minimise them.
items.ms: The time interval is very small, so maximise the distance between the microphones; the other points concern accurately measuring the difference in distance travelled by the sound to each microphone (mark scheme wording partly garbled in the input; 3 marks in total).

items.name: Speed of sound: safety comment
items.how: Comment on safety for the speed of sound experiment.
items.ms: 1 mark for identifying it as a low-risk experiment, or for keeping the sound not too loud to avoid ear damage.

items.name: Criticise diode V-I results table
items.how: Criticise a table of potential difference and current readings for a circuit component.
items.ms: Any 3 from: inconsistent or insufficient significant figures in p.d.; small p.d. range; more readings needed between 0.5 and 1.0 V; only 6 sets of readings; no negative values; no repetition shown.

items.name: Find centre of gravity of bat + Physics and assumptions of balance method
items.how: Explain the physics of your method in (a) and any assumptions made.
items.ms: 1 mark for the relevant physics (when balanced the centre of gravity is vertically below the support or above the knife edge; clockwise moment equals anticlockwise moment) and 1 mark for an assumption (e.g. symmetrical cross-section so centre of gravity is at the centre of the cross-section).

items.name: Plot V-I graph for component + Resistance at 40 mA, graph shape
items.how: (i) Use your graph to determine the resistance at 40 mA (4 marks); (ii) with reference to resistance, explain the shape of the graph between 0 and 0.5 V (2 marks).
items.ms: (i) Read V from own line of best fit at 40 mA, use R = V/I (not the gradient), answer in the range 42.5 to 44.0 ohm with 2 or 3 s.f. and unit. (ii) Resistance very high or infinite, as the component (diode) only conducts when the forward p.d. reaches a specific value, so the current is zero or negligible.

items.name: Non-base SI quantity identification
items.how: Multiple choice: which of amount of substance, electric charge, electric current, thermodynamic temperature is not an SI base quantity.
items.ms: B (electric charge). The other three are SI base quantities.

items.name: Micrometer screw gauge reading
items.how: Multiple choice: read a micrometer screw gauge shown in a diagram.
items.ms: C (21.32 mm). A and B are too low a reading; D is too high.

items.name: Mean motor time, omit anomaly
items.how: Multiple choice on a motor efficiency experiment: which value should be used from times 3.4, 4.5, 3.1, 3.5 s.
items.ms: C (3.3 s): omit the anomalous 4.5 s and quote the mean to an appropriate number of significant figures. A and B include 4.5; B and D have too many s.f.

items.name: Efficiency calculation: quantity not needed
items.how: Multiple choice: which quantity is not needed in the efficiency calculation for the motor raising a mass (stem in Q3).
items.ms: C (density of the mass). Power input, power output and the weight of the mass (to find output power) are all needed.

deps.name: Mean motor time, omit anomaly

items.name: Effect of larger height on uncertainty
items.how: Multiple choice: the experiment is repeated with height 0.90 m and mean time 7.1 s; which statement about uncertainties is correct.
items.ms: D (percentage uncertainty in the time measurement has decreased). Absolute uncertainty depends only on the instrument, so a larger measured value gives a smaller percentage uncertainty (A, B and C wrong).

deps.name: Mean motor time, omit anomaly

items.name: Cube length: instrument, range, percentage uncertainty
items.how: Given mean cube side 1.50 cm +/- 0.05 cm: (i) state the instrument to use (1), (ii) state the range of the measurements (1), (iii) calculate the percentage uncertainty (2).
items.ms: (i) Vernier callipers, digital vernier or micrometer. (ii) 1.45 to 1.55 cm (accept 0.10 cm). (iii) Divide 0.05 (or 0.10) by 1.50 then give about 3% (accept 3.3%, or 7% / 6.7% using 0.10).

items.name: Density of metal cube in SI units
items.how: Determine the density in kg m^-3 of a cube of side 1.50 cm and mass 38.1 g (negligible uncertainty).
items.ms: Use density = mass/volume (1); density 1.13 x 10^4 kg m^-3 (1); give to 2 or 3 s.f. with the x 10^4 power (1). Working: 38.1 x 10^-3 kg / (1.5 x 10^-2 m)^3.

deps.name: Cube length: instrument, range, percentage uncertainty

items.name: emf and internal resistance circuit diagram
items.how: Plan question (e.m.f. and internal resistance of a '1.5 V' cell by a graphical method): draw a circuit diagram.
items.ms: 1 mark for a workable circuit with cell (not battery), resistor, ammeter and voltmeter; 1 mark for a means of varying the current or p.d.

items.name: emf experiment: repeat readings
items.how: Comment on whether repeat readings are appropriate in this case.
items.ms: Either yes (so a mean can be found for each value, or to reduce random errors) or no (because the cell might run down, better to take many readings). Ignore references to heating.

items.name: Graph of p.d. against current, analysis
items.how: Explain how the data collected will be used, including a sketch of the expected graph.
items.ms: 1 mark each: plot p.d. (y-axis) against current (x-axis); sketch showing y-intercept and negative gradient; e.m.f. identified as the intercept; internal resistance identified as the (negative of the) gradient.

deps.name: emf and internal resistance: quantities measured

items.name: emf experiment: uncertainty and systematic error
items.how: Identify the main sources of uncertainty and/or systematic error.
items.ms: Any 2 from: difficulty reading the meters simultaneously; parallax error on an analogue meter; fluctuating meter readings; zero error on a meter.

items.name: emf experiment: safety comment
items.how: Comment on safety.
items.ms: Low risk experiment as only 1.5 V (1 mark).

items.name: Criticise spring extension results
items.how: Criticise a table of load and spring length readings.
items.ms: 1 mark for no repetition shown; 1 mark for only 4 or 5 sets of readings (insufficient number).

items.name: Complete spring results table
items.how: Complete the last row of the table of load, length and extension.
items.ms: Two missing entries, 1 mark each: 39.2 and 66 (load 39.2 N for four 1.0 kg masses, extension 66 mm).

items.name: Why F-extension graph is straight through origin
items.how: Explain why a graph of F (y-axis) against extension (x-axis) should be a straight line through the origin.
items.ms: 1 mark for comparing F = kx with y = mx + c; 1 mark (dependent on the first) for k being constant and c = 0. If nothing else is credited, 1 mark for force being directly proportional to extension.

items.name: Spring graph and force constant
items.how: (i) Plot F against extension on the grid and draw a line of best fit (4 marks); (ii) determine the force constant of the spring (2 marks).
items.ms: (i) 1 mark each: axes labelled with quantities and units; sensible scales; correct plotting; best fit line. (ii) Use a large triangle for the gradient (1); force constant in the range 580 to 610 N m^-1 to 2 or 3 s.f. with unit (1), e.g. 35.5/60 = 0.592 N mm^-1.

deps.name: Complete spring results table

items.name: emf and internal resistance: quantities measured + emf and internal resistance: variables + Choice of measuring instrument, justified
items.how: For one of the quantities listed in (b), explain the choice of measuring instrument.
items.ms: 1 mark for naming ammeter for current or voltmeter for p.d. (multimeter accepted if the scale is mentioned); 1 mark for an appropriate scale or range, e.g. 2 V because the cell is labelled 1.5 V.

items.name: SI base quantity identification
items.how: Multiple choice: which of charge, coulomb, second, time is an SI base quantity.
items.ms: D (time). Charge is not a base quantity; coulomb and second are units.

items.name: Vernier scale reading
items.how: Multiple choice: read a vernier scale shown in a diagram.
items.ms: B (16.4 mm). A does not start from 0 on the small scale; C and D start after the 0 on the small scale.

items.name: Best time value, omit anomaly
items.how: Multiple choice on a tennis ball free-fall experiment: best statement of fall time from 0.96, 0.98, 0.89 and 0.99 s.
items.ms: D (0.98 s): anomalous 0.89 s omitted and mean given to a sensible number of s.f. A and B include the anomaly; C has too many s.f.

items.name: Free fall: quantity also required
items.how: Multiple choice: which further quantity is needed in the free-fall calculation (stem in Q3).
items.ms: A (initial velocity of the ball), needed in the equations of uniformly accelerated motion. Mass, diameter and density are not required.

deps.name: Best time value, omit anomaly

items.name: Free fall: not an error source
items.how: Multiple choice: which is not a possible source of error in the free-fall experiment.
items.ms: D (ball not reaching terminal velocity), since terminal velocity is not reached over such a short fall. Reaction time, zero error and parallax are all sources of error.

deps.name: Best time value, omit anomaly

items.name: Filament lamp I-V circuit diagram
items.how: Draw a circuit diagram for investigating how current varies with p.d. for a filament lamp.
items.ms: 1 mark each: power supply, lamp and ammeter in series; a means of varying the current in the lamp; voltmeter in parallel with the appropriate component (the lamp).

items.name: Advantage of digital meters
items.how: State one advantage of digital meters other than greater accuracy.
items.ms: 1 mark for no parallax error, or easy to switch range.

items.name: Technique for accurate lamp measurements
items.how: Explain another experimental technique (besides checking zero errors) to make the investigation as accurate as possible.
items.ms: Any one technique with its reason, 2 marks: repeat readings and average to reduce random errors; or read I and V simultaneously because digital readings fluctuate; or allow time for the filament temperature to become steady because I or R depend on temperature.

items.name: Glass density: repeat readings
items.how: Comment on whether repeat readings are appropriate.
items.ms: Repeats are appropriate to identify anomalies, deal with random error, or deal with variation in a named measurement (1 mark).

items.name: Accurate measurement of slide thickness
items.how: Suggest how to make the measurement of the slide thickness as accurate as possible.
items.ms: 1 mark for measuring the thickness of all 10 slides together, or at various places or on different slides and averaging; 1 mark for the reason, to reduce the percentage uncertainty.

items.name: Glass density: using measurements
items.how: Explain how the measurements made will be used to determine the density.
items.ms: 1 mark for volume = length x width x thickness; 1 mark for density = mass/volume.

deps.name: Glass density: quantities to measure

items.name: Glass density: uncertainty and systematic error
items.how: State the main sources of uncertainty and/or systematic error.
items.ms: Any 2 from: variation in thickness, length or width of the slides; thickness is a small value; zero error in a named instrument; volume incorrect because of a chip or dust on the slide.

items.name: Glass density: safety
items.how: Comment on safety.
items.ms: 1 mark for a hazard with precaution, e.g. glass can have sharp edges or break so handle with care; do not overtighten the micrometer as the glass might break.

items.name: Criticise resonance tube results
items.how: Criticise a table of tuning fork frequency f and air column length l.
items.ms: Any 2 from: small range or uneven spacing; no repetition shown; only 4 sets of readings; inconsistent s.f. or d.p.

items.name: Why wavelength equals 4l
items.how: Explain why the student calculated the wavelength as 4l for a standing wave in an air column closed at one end by water.
items.ms: 1 mark for an antinode at the open end of the tube and a node at the closed end (water surface); 1 mark for node to antinode distance being lambda/4. A labelled diagram can earn both.

items.name: Glass density: quantities to measure + Glass density: apparatus list + Glass density: instrument choice justified
items.how: For two of the quantities listed in (a), explain the choice of measuring instrument.
items.ms: For each of two quantities: 1 mark for the instrument and 1 mark for a justification that relates its precision to the expected measurement.

items.name: Lambda against 1/f graph, line through origin + Speed of sound from graph gradient
items.how: Use your graph to determine a value for the speed of sound in air.
items.ms: 1 mark for a large triangle covering at least half of the drawn line; 1 mark for a value to 3 s.f., about 327 m s^-1 (range 315 to 339).

items.name: Lambda against 1/f graph, line through origin + Speed of sound from graph gradient + Reason speed differs from accepted value
items.how: Suggest a reason why the calculated value for v may differ from the accepted value.
items.ms: Any one reason: marked frequency may be incorrect; end correction or tube length not exactly lambda/4; speed depends on temperature; difficulty locating the loudest position; parallax in measuring length; poor line of best fit from few points.

items.name: Recording mean wire length, sig figs
items.how: Multiple choice: how to record the mean of 1000, 1002, 999 and 998 mm in a results table (1.0 m, 1.00 m, 1.000 m or 0.999 m).
items.ms: C (1.000 m): the mean 999.75 mm is quoted to the same precision as the readings, i.e. four significant figures.

items.name: Non-pressure unit identification
items.how: Multiple choice: which of kN m^2, N mm^-2, N m^-2, Pa could not be a unit for pressure.
items.ms: A (kN m^2, which lacks the -2 power). The others are valid pressure units.

items.name: Extension proportional to wire length
items.how: Multiple choice: for a wire stretched by a constant force, the extension is directly proportional to which quantity.
items.ms: B (length of the wire), since extension = F L / (A E) at constant force.

items.name: Describing linear V-I relationship
items.how: Multiple choice: describe the relationship between V and I from a graph of p.d. across a power supply against current.
items.ms: C (linear relationship). The mark scheme gives only the letter; the graph is a straight line that is not directly proportional.

items.name: Gradient of V-I graph
items.how: Multiple choice: choose the magnitude of the gradient of the V against I graph (10, 4.6, 2.2 or 0.46).
items.ms: C (2.2). The mark scheme gives only the letter; the gradient magnitude is the supply's internal resistance.

deps.name: Describing linear V-I relationship

items.name: Newcomb c value inconsistent uncertainty
items.how: Given today's accepted c = 299 792.458 +/- 0.001 km/s and Newcomb's 299 850 +/- 30 km/s, explain how his stated uncertainty shows he underestimated his uncertainties.
items.ms: 1 mark for his range 299 820 to 299 880 (or a numerical comparison); 1 mark for a statement that this lies outside the accepted value.

items.name: Comment on Michelson c value
items.how: Comment on Michelson's value of 299 796 +/- 4 km/s compared with the accepted value.
items.ms: Max 2 from: his range 299 792 to 299 800 includes the accepted value (just inside); an appropriate numerical approach (e.g. about 1 x 10^-3 % uncertainty); a comparative statement about the percentage uncertainties.

items.name: Percentage uncertainty in accepted c
items.how: Calculate the percentage uncertainty claimed for today's accepted value of c.
items.ms: 1 mark for an attempt using half the range or whole range; 1 mark for 3.3 x 10^-7 % (or 6.7 x 10^-7 % using the whole range).

items.name: Draw distance s on free fall apparatus
items.how: Plan question (g by timing a falling steel ball, graph of s against t^2): draw on the diagram the distance s to be measured.
items.ms: 1 mark for s drawn as the height from the base of the ball to the trap door (switch X).

items.name: Apparatus to measure fall distance
items.how: State the apparatus required to measure s and explain the choice.
items.ms: 1 mark for a metre rule or tape; 1 mark for justification with reference to the distance fallen and 1 mm divisions.

items.name: Why use electronic timer
items.how: Explain why an electronic timer is used to measure t.
items.ms: The time is too short for reliable measurement by hand or stopwatch, or reaction time is significant compared with the measured time (1 mark).

items.name: Free fall: repeat readings
items.how: Comment on whether repeat readings are appropriate in this case.
items.ms: Max one: repeating and averaging gives a more reliable result; repeating allows anomalies to be identified; comment on the difficulty of hitting the switch or alignment.

items.name: Free fall: s-t squared graph analysis
items.how: Explain what data will be collected and how it will be used to determine g from a graph of s against t^2.
items.ms: 1 mark each: times for at least 5 heights; straight line graph expected (words or labelled sketch); determine the gradient; use s = ut + 1/2 at^2 (or s = 1/2 at^2); multiply the gradient by 2 to get g.

items.name: Free fall: uncertainty and systematic error
items.how: Identify the main sources of uncertainty and/or systematic error.
items.ms: Any 2 from: time taken by the electromagnet to release the ball; parallax in a specified measurement; systematic or zero error on the height or timer.

items.name: Free fall: safety
items.how: Comment on safety.
items.ms: 1 mark for a relevant hazard with a precaution, e.g. low voltage supply and small falling mass so no major hazard; do not tread on the steel ball (slipping); wear shoes against the falling ball.

items.name: Criticise air column frequency results
items.how: Criticise a table of air column length l and frequency f for a musical instrument.
items.ms: Max 2 from: no repeats shown; inconsistent precision in length; only five sets of results or not enough readings.

items.name: Complete 1/l column of table
items.how: Complete the last column of the table with values of 1/l.
items.ms: 1 mark for the unit (m^-1 or cm^-1), 1 mark for correct values (10.0, 8.0, 6.9, 6.1, 5.3 m^-1), 1 mark for consistent decimal places.

items.name: Plot f against 1/l graph + Gradient of f against 1/l graph
items.how: Determine the gradient of your graph.
items.ms: 1 mark for a large triangle; 1 mark for an attempt to calculate the gradient; 1 mark for a value of 172 +/- 5 (m^-1 units) or 17 200 +/- 500 (cm^-1 equivalent), e.g. (1720 - 800)/(10 - 4.75) = 175.

items.name: Calculate speed of sound from gradient + Explain difference from accepted speed
items.how: Given an accepted value of 330 m s^-1, suggest why there is a difference from your value for v, assuming the calculations are correct.
items.ms: Any one: inaccuracy in measuring frequency; error in measuring length; comment on temperature or humidity; variation in playing technique.

items.name: Instrument for wire diameter
items.how: Multiple choice: which instrument measures the diameter of a wire in a Young modulus experiment.
items.ms: C (micrometer screw gauge).

items.name: Mean diameter, omit anomaly
items.how: Multiple choice: which value should be recorded as the mean of 0.27, 0.29, 0.72 and 0.26 mm.
items.ms: D (0.27 mm): the anomalous 0.72 mm is omitted and the mean is given to the precision of the readings.

items.name: SI unit of resistivity
items.how: Multiple choice: which is the SI unit for resistivity (ohm m^-1, ohm m, ohm, m ohm^-1).
items.ms: B (ohm metre).

items.name: Resistivity experiment: measurement not required
items.how: Multiple choice: which wire measurement is not needed to determine resistivity (diameter, length, mass, resistance).
items.ms: C (mass). Diameter (for area), length and resistance are all used in R = rho L / A.

items.name: Reciprocal of wavelength in SI
items.how: Multiple choice in a Planck constant experiment: the correct value of 1/lambda for lambda = 595 nm.
items.ms: D (1.68 x 10^6 m^-1): 1/(595 x 10^-9 m), with correct reciprocal unit.

items.name: Internal resistance circuit diagram
items.how: Draw a circuit diagram using a 1.5 V cell, switch, variable resistor, ammeter and voltmeter to determine internal resistance.
items.ms: Any correct working circuit (1 mark): ammeter in series, voltmeter in parallel across the cell or the total external resistance; a potential divider arrangement is acceptable.

items.name: Why cell experiment low risk
items.how: State why the internal resistance experiment is considered low risk.
items.ms: 1 mark for referring to the low p.d. (only a 1.5 V cell, so very small voltage or no shock risk).

items.name: Why avoid zero variable resistance
items.how: Suggest why the variable resistor should not be reduced to zero.
items.ms: 1 mark: the cell or circuit would be short circuited (and get hot), i.e. a high current would flow through the cell.

items.name: Spring energy: diagram and apparatus
items.how: Plan question (energy stored in a spring extended by 300 mm, graphical method): draw a labelled diagram and list any additional apparatus.
items.ms: 1 mark each: labelled diagram of a workable set-up (spring, mass or weight, support); a rule shown or mentioned; appropriate additional apparatus (e.g. set square, pin, balance), which may appear anywhere in the answer.

items.name: Accurate extension measurement technique
items.how: Describe how to make the measurement of the extension as accurate as possible.
items.ms: Max 2 from: use of a fiducial mark; use of a set square; reading at eye level to avoid parallax error.

items.name: Spring: repeat readings appropriate?
items.how: Comment on whether repeat readings are appropriate in this case.
items.ms: 1 mark for a justified comment, e.g. would not repeat because of permanent extension; or repeat to identify anomalies; or repeat and average for a more accurate result.

items.name: Energy stored from force-extension graph
items.how: Explain how the data collected will be used to determine the energy stored at 300 mm extension.
items.ms: Plot force against extension (1; mass-extension allowed only if conversion to force is explained). Then either area under the graph up to 300 mm using squares or a triangle (3 marks across these points), or read F = 7.5 N at x = 300 mm and use E = Fx/2.

deps.name: Spring energy: independent, dependent variables

items.name: Spring: main source of uncertainty
items.how: Explain the main source of uncertainty and/or systematic error.
items.ms: 1 mark for a reference to measurement of length or extension with the error, e.g. parallax, small measurement, zero error, elastic limit exceeded.

items.name: Spring: safety
items.how: Comment on safety.
items.ms: 1 mark for a sensible risk with precaution, e.g. falling weights so use foot protection; breaking spring so use goggles.

items.name: Unit for 1/d squared
items.how: Add a unit for 1/d^2 to the results table of intensity I against distance d from a light bulb.
items.ms: m^-2 or 1/m^2 (1 mark).

items.name: Criticise inverse square results table
items.how: Criticise the results table.
items.ms: Max 2 from: inconsistent s.f./d.p.; no repeat readings or averaging; large gap between 64 and 16 (poor choice of d values). Just stating poor range gets no mark.

items.name: Complete inverse square table
items.how: Complete the table of d, I and 1/d^2.
items.ms: 1 mark for 1/d^2 = 1.8 (at d = 0.75 m) and 1 mark for 1.0 (at d = 1 m).

items.name: Why I against 1/d2 is linear
items.how: Given I = k/d^2, explain why a graph of I against 1/d^2 should be a straight line through the origin.
items.ms: 1 mark for an explicit or implicit comparison with y = mx (+ c); 1 mark for intensity being directly proportional to 1/d^2, or intercept c being zero.

items.name: Spring energy: independent, dependent variables + Spring energy: measuring instruments chosen
items.how: State and explain the choice of measuring instruments for the independent and dependent variables.
items.ms: For the independent variable: instrument for mass/weight/force (1) with justification by scale (uncertainty or range) and expected measurement (1). For the dependent variable: metre rule (or vernier callipers for extension) (1) with similar justification (1).

items.name: Plot I against 1/d2 graph + Read intensity at 20 cm
items.how: Use your graph to determine I when d = 20 cm.
items.ms: 1 mark for calculating 1/d^2 (25 m^-2, may be implicit); 1 mark for I = 380 to 410 W m^-2 (gradient method accepted).

items.name: SI base quantity identification
items.how: Multiple choice: which of ampere, charge, current, volt is an SI base quantity.
items.ms: No mark scheme for Q1 in the input (only Q8 survives). Worked answer, not from the mark scheme: C (current); ampere and volt are units, and charge is a derived quantity.

items.name: Mean reaction time with uncertainty
items.how: Multiple choice: choose the mean and uncertainty for readings 0.21, 0.19, 0.20 and 0.09 s.
items.ms: No mark scheme for Q2 in the input. Worked answer, not from the mark scheme: B (0.20 +/- 0.01 s), with the anomalous 0.09 s omitted and half-range uncertainty.

items.name: Viscosity experiment: quantity not needed
items.how: Multiple choice on a falling-sphere viscosity experiment: which of liquid density, sphere density, sphere diameter, liquid volume is not needed.
items.ms: No mark scheme for Q3 in the input. Worked answer, not from the mark scheme: D (volume of the liquid); the others appear in the Stokes law and terminal velocity equations.

items.name: Instrument for sphere diameter
items.how: Multiple choice: which instrument should measure the diameter of the sphere (stem in Q3).
items.ms: No mark scheme for Q4 in the input. Worked answer, not from the mark scheme: C (micrometer screw gauge), which suits a small sphere.

deps.name: Viscosity experiment: quantity not needed

items.name: SI unit of viscosity
items.how: Multiple choice: which is the SI unit for viscosity (context in Q3).
items.ms: No mark scheme for Q5 in the input. Worked answer, not from the mark scheme: B (N s m^-2, equivalent to Pa s).

deps.name: Viscosity experiment: quantity not needed

items.name: Microwave standing wave wavelength explanation
items.how: Explain, with a labelled diagram, why the microwave wavelength equals twice the distance between adjacent burn marks (6 cm in the stem). Input text for the question is truncated.
items.ms: No mark scheme for Q6 in the input. Inferred from the wording: burn marks lie at antinodes of the standing wave, adjacent antinodes are lambda/2 apart.

items.name: Instrument for burn mark spacing, percentage uncertainty
items.how: (i) Suggest a suitable instrument for measuring the distance between burn marks and give a reason (2 marks); (ii) calculate the percentage uncertainty in the 6.0 cm distance (marks and rest of the wording cut off in the input).
items.ms: No mark scheme for Q6 in the input. Part (ii) mark allocation cannot be seen, so marks are left null.

items.name: Filament lamp circuit diagram
items.how: Plan question (resistance of a 12 V filament lamp at different p.d.s, graphical method): draw and label a circuit diagram.
items.ms: No mark scheme for Q7 in the input. 2 marks are available for the circuit.

items.name: Lamp experiment: quantities and instruments
items.how: State the quantities to be measured and suggest a suitable measuring instrument for each.
items.ms: No mark scheme for Q7 in the input. 2 marks are available.

items.name: Lamp experiment: repeat readings
items.how: Comment on whether repeat readings are appropriate in this case.
items.ms: No mark scheme for Q7 in the input. 1 mark is available.

items.name: Sketch I-V graph, find resistance
items.how: Sketch the graph to be drawn and explain how the data collected will be used to determine the resistance at a given p.d.
items.ms: No mark scheme for Q7 in the input. 3 marks are available for the sketch and the method.

deps.name: Lamp experiment: quantities and instruments

items.name: Lamp experiment: uncertainty and systematic error
items.how: Identify the main sources of uncertainty and/or systematic error.
items.ms: No mark scheme for Q7 in the input. 2 marks are available.

items.name: Lamp experiment: safety
items.how: Comment on safety.
items.ms: No mark scheme for Q7 in the input. 1 mark is available.

items.name: Criticise wire extension results
items.how: Criticise a table of mass, force and extension for a wire (diameter 0.245 mm, length 1.35 m).
items.ms: 1 mark each: inconsistent s.f./d.p.; no evidence of loading and unloading (or no repetition); more readings needed between 600 g and 1000 g (at the point of curvature).

items.name: Measuring wire diameter technique
items.how: Describe how the student should measure the diameter of the wire.
items.ms: 1 mark for repeating the measurement and calculating the mean; 1 mark for measuring at different positions or orientations along the length.

items.name: Force-extension graph and its shape
items.how: (i) Plot F (y-axis) against extension (x-axis) and draw a line of best fit (5 marks); (ii) comment on the shape of the graph (2 marks).
items.ms: (i) 1 mark each: axes in the correct orientation; with units; sensible scales; correct plotting; best fit line. (ii) Max 2 from: linear up to the limit of proportionality (initially obeys Hooke's law); then curved, with greater extension for equal force increases.

items.name: SI base quantity identification
items.how: Multiple choice: pick the SI base quantity from ampere, charge, current and volt.
items.ms: C (current). Ampere and volt are units, and charge is not a base quantity.

items.name: Reciprocal of wavelength in SI units
items.how: Multiple choice: give the correct value and unit of 1/lambda for lambda = 471 nm (Planck constant experiment).
items.ms: D, 2.12 x 10^6 m^-1. The other options have wrong powers of ten.

items.name: Quantity not needed for resistivity
items.how: Multiple choice: which of density, resistance, area and length is not needed to find the resistivity of a wire.
items.ms: A (density). It is not in rho = RA/l; resistance, area and length are all required.

items.name: Instrument for wire diameter
items.how: Multiple choice: choose the instrument to measure the diameter of a wire about 1 mm across.
items.ms: C (micrometer screw gauge). A metre rule and vernier calipers lack the precision; an electronic balance is irrelevant.

items.name: SI unit of resistivity
items.how: Multiple choice: select the SI unit for resistivity from four forms of ohm and metre.
items.ms: C (ohm metre). Ohm is the unit of resistance, and the other options have the wrong power of metre.

items.name: Range from mean and uncertainty
items.how: State the range of the measurements for a nylon thread diameter reported as 0.150 mm +/- 0.005 mm.
items.ms: 0.145 to 0.155 mm, given to 3 d.p. (1 mark). The width of the range, 0.010 mm, is also allowed.

items.name: Percentage uncertainty in thread diameter
items.how: Calculate the percentage uncertainty in the diameter 0.150 mm +/- 0.005 mm.
items.ms: (0.005/0.150) x 100 = 3.3%. 3% or 7% (half range or full range) is accepted, to 1 or 2 s.f.

items.name: Absolute uncertainty from percentage uncertainty
items.how: Calculate the uncertainty in a hair diameter of 0.075 mm given a 5% percentage uncertainty.
items.ms: 0.075 x 0.05 = 0.0038 mm; 0.004 mm to 1 or 2 s.f. is accepted and the unit is required. Full or half range from (a) and (b) is allowed.

items.name: Independent and dependent variables, falling sphere
items.how: State which is the independent variable and which is the dependent variable.
items.ms: Diameter (or radius) of the sphere and time (or velocity) as the variables (1); independent and dependent correctly assigned (1).

deps.name: Quantities measured in viscosity plan

items.name: Repeat readings for falling sphere
items.how: For one quantity, comment on whether repeat readings are appropriate.
items.ms: Name a quantity and justify, e.g. repeat the diameter at different orientations and average, repeat the times and average, or repeat to identify anomalies.

deps.name: Quantities measured in viscosity plan

items.name: Graph analysis to find viscosity
items.how: Explain how the collected data give the viscosity from v = 2r^2(rho_s - rho_l)g/9eta, and sketch the expected graph.
items.ms: Calculate v for each sphere and r = d/2 (1); plot v against r^2 or sqrt(v) against r (1); sketch with labelled axes and a straight line through the origin (1); use the equation to relate the gradient to eta, consistent with the graph (1).

deps.name: Quantities measured in viscosity plan
Independent and dependent variables, falling sphere

items.name: Uncertainty and systematic error sources
items.how: Identify the main sources of uncertainty and/or systematic error.
items.ms: Any two: terminal velocity not reached before timing; sphere not dropped centrally (edge effects); short fall time so reaction time matters; small diameter gives large percentage uncertainty; zero error on micrometer or rule; parallax.

items.name: Safety in falling sphere experiment
items.how: Comment on safety.
items.ms: A risk with an appropriate precaution, e.g. spilt liquid is a slip hazard so mop it up; stating a safe experiment needing no precautions is also accepted.

items.name: Criticise pendulum results
items.how: Criticise a table of T, T^2 and l readings from a simple pendulum experiment to find g.
items.ms: Any two: small range, no repetition shown, only 5 sets, inconsistent d.p. or s.f., should time more than one oscillation.

items.name: Why T squared against l is linear
items.how: Explain why a graph of T^2 (y-axis) against l (x-axis) should be a straight line through the origin, given T = 2 pi sqrt(l/g).
items.ms: T^2 = (4 pi^2/g) l compared with y = mx + c (1); 4 pi^2/g is constant and c = 0 (1).

items.name: Falling sphere apparatus diagram + Extra instruments for viscosity plan
items.how: List any additional measuring instruments not shown in your diagram.
items.ms: Metre rule (or tape), stopwatch (or light gates), and micrometer or digital calliper.

items.name: Quantities measured in viscosity plan + Justify instruments for two quantities
items.how: For two quantities listed in (c), explain the choice of measuring instrument.
items.ms: 2 marks for naming the quantity with a suitable instrument, and 2 marks for explanations that relate the instrument's precision to the expected measurement.

items.name: Plot T squared against l; gradient and g + Percentage difference from accepted g
items.how: Calculate the percentage difference between the value of g from (c)(iii) and the accepted value.
items.ms: %D = (value from (c)(iii) - 9.81)/9.81 x 100 (1); correct value from the student's own g to 1 or 2 s.f. (1).

items.name: SI base unit identification
items.how: Multiple choice: pick the SI base unit from coulomb, charge, second and time.
items.ms: C (second). Coulomb is a derived unit; charge and time are quantities, not units.

items.name: Reading a microammeter scale
items.how: Multiple choice: read a microammeter scale shown in a diagram and choose the correct reading with its power of ten.
items.ms: C. The option values are garbled in the input; the mark scheme gives only the letter.

items.name: Measurement not needed for Young modulus
items.how: Multiple choice: which measurement is not needed in a loaded-wire Young modulus experiment (diameter, mass of wire, original length, weight of load).
items.ms: B (mass of the wire); the other three are needed for stress and strain.

items.name: Young modulus from stress-strain graph
items.how: Multiple choice: which graph feature gives the Young modulus (area or gradient of force-extension or stress-strain).
items.ms: D, the gradient of a stress against strain graph.

items.name: SI unit of Young modulus
items.how: Multiple choice: select the correct unit for the Young modulus.
items.ms: D (N m^-2; superscripts are lost in the input but this is stress over strain).

items.name: Varying thermistor temperature 0 to 100 C
items.how: Plan for an NTC thermistor resistance-temperature investigation between 0 and 100 C: explain how the temperature will be varied.
items.ms: 1 mark for a means of varying temperature below room temperature and 1 for a means above room temperature.

items.name: Quantities and instruments for thermistor
items.how: State the quantities to be measured, with a suitable instrument for each.
items.ms: Resistance with an ohmmeter, or p.d. and current with suitable meters (2); temperature with a thermometer or suitable sensor (2).

items.name: Variables in thermistor investigation
items.how: Identify the dependent and independent variables.
items.ms: Dependent and independent variables both correctly identified (1); temperature is varied and resistance measured.

deps.name: Quantities and instruments for thermistor

items.name: Why repeat readings unsuitable for thermistor
items.how: Explain why repeat readings are not appropriate in this case.

items.name: Main uncertainty in thermistor temperature

items.ms: Thermometer temperature may differ from the thermistor's temperature (1); minimise by stirring the water, keeping the thermistor in contact with the thermometer, or allowing time to reach thermal equilibrium (1).

items.ms: One improvement with its reason (1 + 1): repeat readings to find a mean or spot anomalies; work in a dark room so the lit LED is clearer; measure wavelength because the manufacturer's data may be uncertain; use more LEDs to increase the range and reduce gradient uncertainty.

items.name: Centre of gravity of cardboard experiment + Why suspension locates centre of gravity
items.how: Explain how your method allows the position of the centre of gravity to be determined.
items.ms: When suspended, C of G is vertically below the support (or above it when balanced) (1) so the weight has no moment (1); alternatively, in equilibrium the resultant moment is zero about any point. 1 mark for stating clockwise moments equal anticlockwise moments.

items.ms: D, 2.12 x 10^6 m^-1. A and B have the wrong power of ten; A and C have the wrong unit.

items.name: Equation for free-fall timing experiment
