items.ms: Take ln f and ln Z values from a point on the best-fit line and substitute with n into c = y - mx, or use similar triangles (1); P is the antilog of c, ln P = c (1); example point (2.65, 36.0) with n = 2.10 gives c = 30.4 and P = 1.59 x 10^13 Hz.

items.name: Choosing instruments for microscope slide dimensions
items.how: Complete a table (4 marks) naming the instrument and its precision for measuring the width and thickness of a slide about 8 cm x 3 cm x 1 mm; the length row (metre rule, 1 mm) is given.
items.ms: One mark per box: width and thickness each need callipers (precision 0.1 or 0.01 mm) or a micrometer (0.01 or 0.001 mm); the precision mark is dependent on a suitable instrument choice.

items.name: Percentage uncertainty in slide length and thickness
items.how: From repeated readings of length and thickness, estimate the percentage uncertainty in each (2 marks).
items.ms: Length 0.13% (half range 0.1 mm / 75.8 mm), or 0.26% using the full range (1); thickness 2% (half range 0.02 mm / 1.00 mm), or 4% using the full range (1).

items.name: Density of glass slide and its uncertainty
items.how: (i) Calculate the density of the slide from its mean dimensions and mass 4.82 g +/- 0.03 g (2 marks); (ii) estimate the percentage uncertainty in the density, taking the width uncertainty as negligible (2 marks).
items.ms: (i) Use of density = mass/volume (1); 2.46 g cm^-3 (2460 kg m^-3) to 3 sf with unit (1). (ii) Percentage uncertainty in mass (0.03/4.82) (1); add it to their length and thickness percentages from (b) (1); example 0.6% + 2% + 0.13% = 2.75%. The MS also has (iii) comparing with a Crown glass density range of 2500 to 2700 kg m^-3 (2), whose text is not in the input.

deps.name: Percentage uncertainty in slide length and thickness

items.name: Why stack of ten slides improves thickness
items.how: Explain why measuring the thickness of a stack of 10 slides gives a better value for one slide's thickness (2 marks).
items.ms: The percentage uncertainty is reduced (1) because the measured value is larger, or a mean over 10 slides is taken, or one slide might be anomalous (1).

items.name: Apparatus to check radioactive source labels
items.how: Planning to check labels 'beta emitter only' and 'range in air' on a source: state the apparatus (1 mark).
items.ms: GM tube and counter (a rate-meter is accepted for both) and a metre rule or absorbers (1).

items.name: Safety handling a radioactive source
items.how: Comment on safety (1 mark) when using the radioactive source.
items.ms: Use handling tools (tongs) (1).

items.name: Resonance curve for electrical circuit
items.how: From plotted V (mV) against f (kHz) data for an electrical resonance: (i) draw a line of best fit (2 marks); (ii) estimate the maximum V (1 mark); (iii) state the resonant frequency (1 mark).
items.ms: (i) A smooth curve passing close to all the points (1) with the maximum clearly below 25 kHz by eye (1). (ii) Maximum V between 27 and 35 mV, with unit (1). (iii) Peak frequency read correctly, with unit, from their curve (1).

items.name: Improve accuracy of resonant frequency
items.how: Suggest one way the experiment could be improved to obtain a more accurate resonant frequency (1 mark).
items.ms: Take more readings of f near the peak (1).

deps.name: Resonance curve for electrical circuit

items.name: Measuring amplitude of damped pendulum
items.how: (i) Explain, with an added diagram, how to measure the amplitude of a pendulum damped by a paper cone using the rule shown (2 marks); (ii) state the expected uncertainty in amplitude measurements (1 mark).
items.ms: (i) Diagram showing the displaced cone (1) and an indication of either edge of the cone as the point of measurement, dependent on the first mark (1). (ii) A value in the range 5 mm to 10 mm (1).

items.name: Show ln A against n is linear
items.how: Given A = A0 e^(-kn), show that a graph of ln A against n should be a straight line (2 marks).
items.ms: Take logs to get ln A = ln A0 - kn (1); compare with y = mx + c and state that -k is the gradient (1).

items.name: Plot ln A against n, find k
items.how: (i) Process the A and n data and draw a graph of ln A against n (5 marks); (ii) use the graph to determine k (2 marks).
items.ms: (i) Ln values correct in the table to 3 sf (1); axes labelled e.g. n and ln(A/cm) (1); scales (1); plots (1); best-fit line (1). (ii) Large triangle using half the plotted line (1); k between 0.0520 and 0.0550 to 3 sf (1).

deps.name: Show ln A against n is linear

items.name: Measurements to check beta-only and range + Technique to reduce count uncertainty + Using measurements to verify source labels
items.how: Explain how these measurements should be used to check that the labels are correct (3 marks).
items.ms: Range method (max 3): count rate should not change at short range (about 5 cm), hence no alpha (dependent); count rate falls to background at around 25 cm, hence no gamma (dependent). Absorber method (max 3): no drop in count rate with paper, hence no alpha; count rate drops to background with lead, hence no gamma.

items.name: Metre rule suitability, band volume
items.how: Explain why a metre rule is suitable for measuring a band length of about 10 cm (2), then calculate the band volume V1 = 2Lwt from measured L, w and t (2, calculation text not captured in the input).
items.ms: (i) Resolution of metre rule is 1 mm, so percentage uncertainty on about 10 cm is about 1%, small and acceptable (1+1). (ii) V1 = 2 x 10.0 x 0.933 x 0.103 = 1.92 cm3, correct to 3 s.f. (1+1).

items.name: Bung height measurement, volume and uncertainty
items.how: Describe how callipers should be used to measure the bung height h (2), then calculate V2 from the frustum formula using mean h (2) and find its percentage uncertainty (1); only (i) is in the captured question text.
items.ms: (i) Callipers held parallel to h with jaws on top and bottom of bung (1); repeat at different orientations for a mean, or do not compress, or check zero error (1). (ii) Mean h = 3.51 cm gives V2 = 29.2 cm3 (2). (iii) %U in V2 equals %U in h, about 0.6% (half range) or 1.1% (range) (1).

items.name: Plan: burette exponential drain, find b
items.how: Write a plan, marked holistically, to find b in V = V0 exp(-t/b) for a burette with V0 = 100 cm3: how to measure V and t with two precautions (4), one source of uncertainty (1), and the graph plotted and how b is found (2).
items.ms: Stopwatch for t and record V at regular time intervals (or time to reach set volumes) (1+1); any two precautions such as repeat for mean, eye level and bottom of meniscus, tap fully open, burette vertical (2). Uncertainty: reading two instruments at once, or liquid below the tap (1). Plot ln V against t (1) with gradient = -1/b (1).

items.name: Effect of lower viscosity on b
items.how: Explain the effect on the value of b when heating the liquid reduces its viscosity.
items.ms: Lower viscosity increases the flow rate (less time for a given volume, or more volume in a given time) (1); so b decreases (1), second mark only after an attempt at the first.

items.name: Thermistor resistance-temperature apparatus diagram
items.how: Draw a labelled diagram of school-lab apparatus to measure how thermistor resistance changes with temperature.
items.ms: Thermistor in a water bath with an identified heat source (1); a means of measuring resistance, such as voltmeter and ammeter circuit or ohmmeter (1); thermometer close to the fully submerged thermistor (1).

items.name: Extra readings and wider temperature range
items.how: Given five resistance readings (in kilohms) across a temperature range, suggest why extra readings between 14 and 45 degrees C help (1) and how the range could be extended (1).
items.ms: (i) Resistance changes by a large amount over this region of lower temperatures, so more points are needed to define the curve (1). (ii) Use ice for lower temperatures or continue heating for higher (1).

items.name: Densities of rubber band and bung + Compare densities: same rubber?
items.how: Comment on whether the band and bung are the same rubber, using the given 4% uncertainty in the band density and the densities calculated in (c).
items.ms: Percentage difference between the densities is about 27% (1); this is far greater than the percentage uncertainty so probably not the same rubber (1). Alternative: compare maximum band density with minimum bung density using the uncertainties.

items.name: SHM trolley: T squared graph, k and M + Accuracy of trolley mass from graph
items.how: Comment on the accuracy of the trolley mass found in (a)(iii) by comparing it with the balance reading of 1.05 kg.
items.ms: Calculate the percentage difference from 1.05 kg (about 6.7% for 1.12 kg) (1); comment that this is comparable with expected uncertainties and plots lie close to the best-fit line, so reasonably accurate (1).

items.name: Lens diameter measurement and percentage uncertainty
items.how: Draw how to measure lens diameter with a half-metre rule and two set squares (1), describe how to check the diameter is uniform (1), and calculate the percentage uncertainty in d = 3.9 cm +/- 0.1 cm (1).
items.ms: Lens on the rule with set-square bases on the rule's edge and their sides against the lens (1); measure the diameter in different orientations (1); %U = 0.1/3.9 x 100 = 2.6% (1).

items.name: Lens thickness, focal length and uncertainty
items.how: Calculate the percentage uncertainty in t = 0.26 cm +/- 0.01 cm (1) and the focal length f = d^2/(8t(mu-1)) with mu = 1.52 (3); the mark scheme also has parts for %U and absolute uncertainty in f and which variable dominates (6 marks, text not captured).
items.ms: (i) 3.8%. (ii) Correct substitution, f = 14 cm, quoted to 2 s.f. with unit (3). Then %U in f = 2 x 2.6 + 3.8 = 9.0% (2), uncertainty about 1.3 cm (1), and d contributes most because its percentage uncertainty is doubled (squared) (2).

deps.name: Lens diameter measurement and percentage uncertainty

items.name: Accurate period of bung in circular motion
items.how: Describe how to obtain an accurate value of the period T (about 1 s) of a bung whirled in a horizontal circle.
items.ms: Use a fiducial marker for counting rotations (1); time several rotations and divide by the number of rotations to get T (1); repeat and calculate a mean (1).

items.name: Derive T squared formula, choose linear graph
items.how: Show that T^2 = 4pi^2 m x/(M g) from Mg = m x omega^2 (2), then state the graph to plot to get a straight line (1).
items.ms: Use omega = 2pi/T (1) and rearrange correctly for T^2 (1). Plot T^2 against 1/M (symbol garbled in the extracted mark scheme), or any other combination of these variables giving a straight line (1).

items.name: Measure string length x with metre rule
items.how: Describe how a metre rule should be used to measure the length x of string below the tube, to the centre of the bung.
items.ms: String taut/straight (1); measure from the end of the tube to the centre of the bung with the mark level with the tube bottom, or from the mark to the bung centre and subtract the tube length (1).

items.name: Safety in rotating bung experiment
items.how: Comment on safety in the whirling-bung experiment.
items.ms: Identify a risk with its matching precaution, e.g. bung may hit the experimenter so wear goggles or use an open space; hanging mass may fall so wear foot protection (1).

items.name: Extra apparatus for force on conductor
items.how: Plan part (holistic): list the additional apparatus needed, beyond the top-pan balance, U-magnet, copper rod and wires, to investigate force against current.
items.ms: Ammeter and d.c. power supply (1); variable resistor or variable power supply (1).

items.name: Circuit diagram for current through rod
items.how: Draw a circuit diagram for supplying and measuring the current in the copper rod.
items.ms: Components connected in series with the copper rod to give a workable circuit (1).

deps.name: Extra apparatus for force on conductor

items.name: Balance, magnet and rod arrangement diagram
items.how: Draw the arrangement of the top-pan balance, U-shaped magnet and conductor so the force can be measured.
items.ms: Magnet on the top-pan balance with the rod suspended between the poles (1); field between the poles perpendicular to the rod (1).

items.name: Procedure: force on conductor against current
items.how: Describe how the investigation is performed, using the circuit and balance arrangement planned in the earlier parts.
items.ms: Take the initial balance reading or check zero error (1); switch on, record the ammeter reading and new balance reading (1); multiply the mass change by g to get the force (1).

deps.name: Circuit diagram for current through rod
Balance, magnet and rod arrangement diagram

items.name: Sketch graph of force against current
items.how: Sketch the graph of expected results for the investigation.
items.ms: Graph of force against current drawn as a straight line through the origin (1).

deps.name: Procedure: force on conductor against current

items.name: Show ln A against t is linear
items.how: Show that a graph of ln A against t should be a straight line, given A = A0 exp(-lambda t).
items.ms: Take logs to get ln A = ln A0 - lambda t (1); compare with y = mx + c, with gradient = -lambda (1).

items.name: ln activity graph, two isotopes, decay constant
items.how: Plot ln(total activity) against time for a source of isotopes X and Y, adding a processed-data column (5, curved graph expected), then use the gradient in a suitable region to find lambda for the longer-lived isotope X (3).
items.ms: ln values to 3 s.f., labelled axes with units, scales, accurate plots, shallow curve as best-fit line (5). Triangle over at least t = 16 to 23 hours (late region where Y is negligible), gradient about -0.073 to -0.080, lambda positive to 2 s.f. in hour-1 (3).

deps.name: Show ln A against t is linear

items.name: Why repeat diameter readings and average
items.how: State why several measurements of the disc diameter are taken and a mean calculated (vernier calipers, 35.2 mm +/- 0.1 mm).
items.ms: To minimise random error, or because the diameter may not be uniform (1).

items.name: Mean thickness and its percentage uncertainty
items.how: From five micrometer readings in mm (1.52 to 1.58), calculate the mean thickness (1) and its percentage uncertainty (2).
items.ms: Mean = 1.55 mm (1); half range = 0.03 mm (or full range 0.06 mm) (1); %U = 1.94% (3.87% if range used) (1).

items.name: Disc volume and its percentage uncertainty
items.how: Calculate the mean disc volume from the mean diameter and thickness (2), then the percentage uncertainty in the volume (3, wording truncated in the input).
items.ms: V = pi r^2 x thickness (1), about 1510 mm3 (1). %U in diameter 0.28% (1), doubled to 0.56% for area (1), added to thickness %U to give about 2.5% (1); error carried forward from (b) allowed.

deps.name: Why repeat diameter readings and average
Mean thickness and its percentage uncertainty

items.name: Density of steel from mass and volume
items.how: Calculate the density of the steel from the disc mass of 11.96 g (negligible uncertainty) and the volume found earlier.
items.ms: Use density = m/V (1); about 7.92 x 10^3 kg m-3 (7.92 g cm-3 accepted) (1), with error carried forward from (c)(i).

deps.name: Disc volume and its percentage uncertainty

items.name: Could the disc be carbon steel?
items.how: Determine whether the disc could be carbon steel (7860 kg m-3), using the measured density and its uncertainty.
items.ms: Lower limit of measured density about 7720 kg m-3 (1), below 7860 so could be carbon steel (1). Alternative: %D = 0.76% is less than %U so could be carbon steel; second mark depends on the first.

deps.name: Disc volume and its percentage uncertainty
Density of steel from mass and volume

items.name: Meaning of precision, stopwatch
items.how: State what is meant by precision for a stopwatch reading to 0.01 s.
items.ms: The smallest measuring interval on an instrument (1).

items.name: Plan: pendulum g from T squared graph
items.how: Write a plan, marked holistically, using T = 2pi sqrt(l/g): diagram showing l (1), one source of uncertainty in T (1), how to get an accurate T (4), and the graph plotted and how g is found (2).
items.ms: Setup with l from support to centre of bob (1); uncertainty such as reaction time starting and stopping the stopwatch (1); time nT and divide by n, repeat for mean, marker at centre of oscillation, start after a few swings or use small amplitude (4); plot T^2 against l and g = 4pi^2/gradient (2), or T against sqrt(l) with g = 4pi^2/gradient^2 (root sign garbled in the extracted mark scheme).

items.name: Precaution for accurate light meter readings
items.how: State a precaution that makes the light-meter measurement of intensity from a filament bulb as accurate as possible.
items.ms: Any means of preventing background light from reaching the light meter (1).

items.name: Metre rule suitability with uncertainty calculation
items.how: Explain, with a calculation, why a metre rule suits measuring distances from 5 cm to 80 cm.
items.ms: Rule resolution is 1 mm (1); in the smallest distance of 50 mm this is a %U of 1/50 x 100 = 2%, which is reasonable (1).

items.name: Test inverse square law from intensity data
items.how: Explain, with calculations, whether three (d, I) readings are consistent with I = k d^-2.
items.ms: Rearrange to k = I d^2 (1); compute three k values, about 8.0, 7.9, 8.1 (1); comment that k is constant within small variation so the data are consistent (1).

items.name: Liquid property controlling flow rate
items.how: State the property of the liquid that determines the rate at which it flows from the burette.
items.ms: Viscosity (1).

items.name: Advantage of opening tap above zero mark
items.how: Suggest one advantage of opening the tap while the initial liquid level is above the zero mark.
items.ms: Avoids the difficulty of opening the tap and starting the timer at exactly the same moment (1).

items.name: Why ln V against t is linear
items.how: Explain why a graph of ln V against t should be a straight line if V = V0 exp(-bt).
items.ms: ln V = ln V0 - bt, compared with y = c + mx (1); gradient = -b, which is constant (1).

items.name: ln V against t graph, find b
items.how: Plot ln V against t from six (V, t) readings, using an extra column for processed data (5), then determine b from the graph (3).
items.ms: ln(V/cm3) values to 3 or 4 s.f., axes labelled ln(V/cm3) and t/s, scales, accurate plots, best-fit line (5). Large triangle, gradient calculation, b stated positive with unit s-1 and 2 or 3 s.f. (about 0.030 s-1) (3); intercept method also accepted.

deps.name: Why ln V against t is linear

items.name: Systematic error, repeats, volume of tennis ball
items.how: State what a systematic error is (1) and comment on whether repeat measurements of a tennis ball diameter are appropriate (2); the mark scheme also has the percentage uncertainty in d from repeats (2) and the volume with its uncertainty (3), text not captured in the input.
items.ms: Systematic error adds a constant amount to every measurement (1). Repeats are appropriate to reduce random error, as the ball may not be uniform, or to remove anomalies (2). Half range gives %U of d = 0.46% (2); V = 4/3 pi r^3 = 149 cm3, %U = 3 x 0.46 = 1.4%, so V = 149 +/- 2 cm3 (3).

items.name: Packing fraction of tennis balls in tube
items.how: Show that four balls in a tube of length l and internal diameter d have packing fraction 2/3 (3); the mark scheme also has a part that calculates the measured packing fraction with its uncertainty and compares it with 2/3 (4), text not captured.
items.ms: Tube volume = pi r^2 l with l = 8r (1+1), then algebra 4(4/3 pi r^3)/(8 pi r^3) = 2/3 (1). Measured packing fraction about 0.58 with %U about 4.2% (1+1); upper limit 0.60 is below 0.67 (or %D = 13% exceeds %U), so not 2/3 (1+1).

deps.name: Systematic error, repeats, volume of tennis ball

items.name: Compare accuracy of two ramp-angle methods
items.how: Explain whether Student A (protractor, 5 degrees) or Student B (s = 1.000 m and h = 8.7 cm with a metre rule) gets the more accurate ramp angle.
items.ms: Resolution of protractor 1 degree (0.5 accepted) and of metre rule 1 mm (1); %U in alpha = 1/5 x 100 = 20% (1); %U in h/s = 0.1/8.7 x 100 + 0.1/100 x 100 = about 1.2% (1); B is more accurate as its %U is smaller (1).

items.name: Measuring horizontal range x in sand tray
items.how: Describe how the horizontal distance x travelled by the marble should be measured, adding to the diagram if wished.
items.ms: Mark a zero point in the sand directly below the table edge using a metre rule and set square or plumb line (or align the tray edge with the table edge) (1); measure the perpendicular distance to the marble's centre (1).

items.name: Definition of resonance
items.how: State what is meant by resonance, in the context of a driven vibrating string.
items.ms: Driving frequency is at or close to the natural frequency (1); maximum energy transfer, giving maximum amplitude (1).

items.name: Does f squared against m graph support prediction?
items.how: Discuss whether a plotted graph of f^2 against m supports the prediction f = k sqrt(m).
items.ms: f^2 = k^2 m is of the form y = mx (+c), so f^2 is directly proportional to m (1); a straight line supports this (1); but the line should pass through the origin, and the graph has a non-zero intercept (1), so it does not fully support the prediction, with an extra constant or systematic error (1).

items.name: Why lamp stays dark in diode circuit
items.how: Explain why the lamp did not light as the slider moved from A to B, although no component was faulty (3); the mark scheme also has a one-mark correction to the circuit (text not captured).
items.ms: Voltmeter has very large resistance (1) so p.d. across the diode is too small (1) and the diode does not conduct, so no current in the lamp (1); correction: place the voltmeter in parallel with the diode, or remove it (1).

items.name: Why ln I against V is linear
items.how: Explain why plotting ln I against V gives a straight line for I = a exp(bV).
items.ms: ln I = bV + ln a (1); compare with y = mx + c, so the gradient b is constant (1); second mark dependent on the first.

items.name: ln I against V graph, find b
items.how: Plot ln I against V for six diode readings with a processed-data column (5), then determine b from the graph (2).
items.ms: ln(I/mA) values to 3 s.f., axes ln(I/mA) and V/V, suitable scales, accurate plots within 1 mm, best-fit line (5). Large triangle (or intercept plus a point over halfway) and b to 2 or 3 s.f. with unit V-1, about 33 V-1 (2).

deps.name: Why ln I against V is linear

items.name: Metre rule precision, measuring can diameter
items.how: State the precision of a metre rule (1) and describe, with a diagram, how two set squares and a metre rule measure the external diameter of a can accurately (2).
items.ms: Precision 1 mm (0.5 mm not accepted) (1). Can on its side with two vertical set squares touching the can and the rule; elevation or plan diagram accepted; 2 marks for a correct working diagram, 1 mark for correct use of two set squares.

items.name: External volume and density of can metal
items.how: From tabulated height, diameter and internal volume readings, show the external volume is about 400 cm3 (1), then calculate the metal volume (1) and, per the mark scheme, the metal density using the mass 4.982 x 10^-2 kg (2); (b)(ii) begins with 'Hence'.
items.ms: V = pi (7.2/2)^2 x 10.1 = 411 cm3 (1); metal volume = 411 - 396 = 15 cm3 (1); density = 49.82 g/15 cm3 = 3.3 g cm-3 (3300 kg m-3) with 2 s.f. and unit (2); error carried forward allowed.

items.name: Uncertainties in can volumes
items.how: Estimate the percentage uncertainty in the external volume, ignoring height uncertainty (2); the mark scheme also has the percentage uncertainty in internal volume (1) and a comment on why the metal volume is poorly determined (1).
items.ms: Half range (or range) gives %U in diameter 1.4% (2.8%), doubled for volume, 2.8% (5.6%) (2). Internal volume %U about 1% (2%) (1). Subtracting two close volumes leaves a small value with a large percentage uncertainty (1).

deps.name: External volume and density of can metal

items.name: Plan: spring constant from T squared graph
items.how: Describe how to make the period readings as accurate as possible (2), and the graph to plot for a straight line and how to get the spring constant from T = 2pi sqrt(m/k) (3).
items.ms: Record nT and divide by n, timing marker at the midpoint/equilibrium, repeat for a mean (max 2). Plot T^2 against m (1), compare with y = mx (+c) (1), k = 4pi^2/gradient (1); alternatives T against sqrt(m) (k = 4pi^2/gradient^2) or ln T against ln m.

items.name: Position sensor and datalogger for period
items.how: Draw how a position sensor and datalogger record the hanging mass's position (2) and explain how this improves measurement of the period compared with the stopwatch (2).
items.ms: Spring and masses with the sensor vertically below, connected to a datalogger (dependent mark) (2). Any two of: readings displayed graphically, removes reaction-time error, precision of T better than 0.01 s (2).

items.name: Criticise LED results
items.how: Criticise a table of four (f, V) results for LEDs used to find Planck's constant.
items.ms: Any one of: no repeats, only four values, no estimate of uncertainty (1).

items.name: LED graph: best fit line, Planck constant
items.how: Draw a best-fit line on a plotted V against f graph (1) and use its gradient with eV = hf - b to find Planck's constant (4); the mark scheme also compares the result with the accepted value (1).
items.ms: Good straight line, not through both top and bottom points (1). Large triangle at least half the line, valid gradient, multiply by e, h about 7.7 to 8.2 x 10^-34 J s to 3 s.f. with unit (4). Percentage difference from 6.63 x 10^-34 J s, about 19% (1).

items.name: Circuit to vary and measure bulb power
items.how: Draw a circuit diagram to vary and determine the electrical power supplied to a bulb.
items.ms: Supply, bulb, voltmeter and ammeter correctly connected (1); a means of varying power, a variable supply or variable resistor (1).

items.name: LDR resistance and constant distance
items.how: State what happens to LDR resistance as light intensity increases (1) and why the LDR-bulb distance must stay constant (1).
items.ms: Resistance decreases (1). Intensity varies with distance, so intensity then depends only on the power supplied (1).

items.name: Power law intensity-power: ln graph, find x
items.how: Show ln I against ln P is linear for I = kP^x (2), plot it from a table of P and I with processed columns (5), and find x from the graph (2); only (i) is in the captured text.
items.ms: ln I = x ln P + ln k, compared with y = mx + c, gradient x constant (2). ln values to 3 or 4 s.f., axes, scales, plots, best-fit line (5). Big triangle and x in the range 2.38 to 2.48 with no unit (2).

items.name: Instrument choice for pipe internal diameter
items.how: State a suitable instrument to measure the internal diameter (about 1 cm) of the pipe (1) and explain the choice (2); the mark scheme also has a one-mark precaution part (iii) not captured in the input.
items.ms: Vernier or digital calipers (1); precision 0.1 mm or 0.01 mm (1), so the expected %U of 1% or 0.1% is small (1). Part (iii): check zero error, or take readings at different orientations and average (1).

items.name: Percentage uncertainty in pipe diameter
items.how: Calculate the percentage uncertainty in the mean internal diameter of 0.995 cm +/- 0.003 cm.

items.name: Viscosity units, value and uncertainty
items.how: Using tabulated values and percentage uncertainties for V/t, P and L, show the unit of viscosity is N s m-2 (2), calculate eta from V/t = pi P r^4/(8 eta L) (2) and find its percentage uncertainty (2).
items.ms: Units: V/t in m3 s-1, L in m, P in N m-2, r^4 in m4 (2), or via Stokes' law with F in N, r in m, v in m s-1. eta about 9.8 x 10^-3 N s m-2 (2). %U = 4 x %U(d) + 3.5 + 0.7 + 0.5 = 5.9% (2); error carried forward from (b).

deps.name: Percentage uncertainty in pipe diameter

items.name: Accurate period of rotational pendulum
items.how: Describe how the student uses a stopwatch (0.01 s), optical pin and metre rule to obtain accurate values of the period T of the rotational pendulum.
items.ms: Pin/marker at the midpoint (equilibrium) of the oscillation (1); record the time for n oscillations and divide by n (1); repeat and calculate a mean (1).

items.name: Straight-line graph for rotational pendulum, find K
items.how: From the given formula for T with constants I and K, describe the graph of T against wire length L that gives a straight line (2) and state how the graph determines K (1); the extracted formula is partly garbled.
items.ms: Plot a power of T (T^2) against L, or the equivalent T against sqrt(L), with the gradient expressed in terms of the constants (2; superscripts garbled in the extracted mark scheme). K from 4pi^2 over the gradient, consistent with the gradient in (i) (1).

items.name: Light gate and datalogger improve period accuracy
items.how: Describe how a light gate attached to a data logger would improve the accuracy of the period measurement.
items.ms: Eliminates the effect of reaction time (1); so the percentage uncertainty is reduced (1), second mark dependent on the first.

items.name: Resonance curve: best fit, peak V, f0
items.how: On a graph of maximum microphone p.d. V against frequency f for a bottle, draw a best-fit line (2), estimate the maximum V (1) and state the resonant frequency f0 (1).
items.ms: Smooth curve passing close to all points (1), with a maximum in the range the mark scheme gives (printed as 101.2 to 101.5 Hz, probably powers of ten on a log axis) (1); correct readings of V maximum (1) and f0 (1) from the graph.

items.name: More readings near resonance peak
items.how: Suggest how taking more readings between 100 Hz and 102 Hz (printed values) increases the accuracy of f0 from the graph.
items.ms: A more accurate best-fit line can be drawn around the peak (1).

deps.name: Resonance curve: best fit, peak V, f0

items.name: Error removed by background subtraction
items.how: State the type of error avoided by subtracting the background count rate from each protactinium reading.
items.ms: Systematic error (1).

items.name: Control variable in decay experiment
items.how: Identify a variable that must be kept constant when measuring the count rate from the sample with a GM tube.
items.ms: Distance between the source (protactinium sample) and the GM tube (1); references to background count rate are ignored.

items.name: Show ln A against t is linear
items.how: Show that a graph of ln A against t should be a straight line, given A = A0 exp(-lambda t) with A as the measured count rate.
items.ms: ln A = ln A0 - lambda t (1); compare with y = mx + c, with gradient = -lambda (1).

items.name: Half-life and comparison with accepted value
items.how: Calculate the half-life of protactinium-234 from t1/2 = ln 2/lambda (1); the mark scheme also compares it with the accepted value of 1.2 minutes (2), text not captured.
items.ms: t1/2 consistent with lambda from (e), about 73 s, with unit (1). Percentage difference from 72 s, about 1.8% (1), and a consistent comment that the value is accurate since the difference is small (1).

deps.name: Decay constant from graph gradient

items.name: Plot ln count rate against time + Decay constant from graph gradient
items.how: Use the graph drawn in (d) to determine a value for the decay constant lambda.
items.ms: Two points from the best-fit line and a large triangle (2); gradient about -9.2 x 10^-3 to -1.1 x 10^-2 (1); lambda positive with unit s-1 and 3 s.f., about 9.4 x 10^-3 s-1 (1).

items.name: Micrometer choice and diameter uncertainty
items.how: Practical-skills part on a wire of approx 0.5 mm diameter: (i) Explain why a micrometer screw gauge is appropriate (2); the mark scheme also covers (ii) a precaution/technique for accurate readings (2) and (iii) the percentage uncertainty in the diameter (1), which are not in the extracted question text.
items.ms: (i) State the micrometer resolution (0.01 mm or 0.001 mm) and show the resulting percentage uncertainty (about 2% or 0.2%) is small. (ii) Check for zero error or use the ratchet to avoid squashing the wire, and take repeat readings at different orientations/places along the wire and average. (iii) %U in diameter = 0.003 mm / 0.275 mm x 100 = 1.1% (1 or 3 s.f. accepted).

items.name: Wire resistivity and its percentage uncertainty
items.how: (i) Calculate the resistivity of the metal from length 0.800 m +/- 0.001 m and resistance 6.48 ohm +/- 0.03 ohm (diameter from part a) (2); the mark scheme also has (ii) the percentage uncertainty in the resistivity (3), not in the extracted text.
items.ms: (i) Use R = rho l / A with A = pi (d/2)^2 (d = 0.275 mm) to get 4.81 x 10^-7 ohm m, 3 s.f. only. (ii) Show %U in R (0.46%) and l (0.13%), double the %U in diameter (2 x 1.1%, ecf from 1(a)(iii)) and add to get 2.8%.

deps.name: Micrometer choice and diameter uncertainty

items.name: Identify wire metal from uncertainty limits
items.how: Explain which of four metals in a resistivity table (constantan, copper, mild steel, nichrome) the wire is most likely made from, using the student's measured resistivity and its uncertainty.
items.ms: Use the %U (2.8%) to calculate upper and/or lower limits (e.g. 4.81 x 10^-7 x 1.028 = 4.94 x 10^-7 ohm m) and compare with the table, or calculate the percentage difference (1.8%) and compare it with the %U; conclude the metal is constantan (4.9 x 10^-7 ohm m). Three marks: limit/difference calculation, comparison comment, correct metal.

deps.name: Wire resistivity and its percentage uncertainty

items.name: Frequency from oscilloscope time-base trace
items.how: Show that the frequency of a signal-generator output is about 6.7 Hz, given an oscilloscope trace with one horizontal division = 50 ms.
items.ms: Read the period from the trace (T = 150 ms) and use f = 1/T (1); f = 1 / (150 x 10^-3 s) = 6.67 Hz, the second mark depending on a correctly shown unit conversion (1).

items.name: Plan graph to verify impedance-frequency relationship
items.how: Write a plan (marked holistically) to verify Z^2 = 4 pi^2 L^2 f^2 + K^2 graphically, where Z = V/I for a coil on a variable-frequency supply; must cover (i) additional components, (ii) measurements, (iii) how they are used, (iv) a sketch of the expected graph.
items.ms: (i) Ammeter and voltmeter (1). (ii) p.d. and current at corresponding frequencies/time periods, frequency from the generator or oscilloscope period (2). (iii) Calculate Z = V/I, then Z^2 and f^2 (3). (iv) Sketch of Z^2 against f^2 as a straight line with a positive y-intercept (K^2) (1).

items.name: Gradient of p against 1/V graph
items.how: Determine the gradient of a given straight-line graph of pressure p (kPa) against 1/V (x 10^5 per m^3) for air in a syringe.
items.ms: Use of a large triangle (1); gradient = 0.30 Pa m^3, e.g. (210 x 10^3 - 0) / (7.0 x 10^5 - 0); 3.0 x 10^-4 kPa m^3 with unit is also accepted (1).

items.name: Number of air molecules from pV = NkT
items.how: Calculate the number of air molecules in the syringe, given the investigation was at 25 deg C and the p against 1/V graph has been drawn.
items.ms: Use pV = NkT with pV equal to the gradient from (a) and T = 298 K (1); N = 0.30 / (1.38 x 10^-23 x 298) = 7.3 x 10^19, ecf from (a), no unit (1).

deps.name: Gradient of p against 1/V graph

items.name: Polarising filters: constant distance, main uncertainty
items.how: Two State questions on a polaroid-filter investigation with lamp, filters and light meter: (i) why the lamp-to-meter distance should be constant (1); (ii) the main source of uncertainty (1).
items.ms: (i) Light intensity varies with distance (inverse square law), so the intensity at the meter would otherwise change. (ii) Background (ambient) light.

items.name: Log-log analysis of polaroid intensity law
items.how: For I = k (cos theta)^n: (i) Explain why log I against log(cos theta) gives a straight line (2); the mark scheme also covers (ii) processing data and plotting the log-log graph (6), (iii) finding n (2) and (iv) finding k (2), which are not in the extracted question text.
items.ms: (i) log I = n log(cos theta) + log k is of the form y = mx + c with constant gradient n. (ii) log I and log(cos theta) correct to 3 or 4 s.f. (ln accepted), labelled axes, suitable scales, plots within 1 mm, best-fit line extended to the y-axis. (iii) n from a large-triangle gradient (about 1.4, positive, no unit). (iv) k from the y-intercept (log k about 2.68, k about 479 lux) or from a point on the line using n, ecf.

items.name: Vernier length uncertainty and measurement precaution
items.how: Tile of side about 20 mm measured with vernier calipers and micrometer: (i) Estimate the percentage uncertainty in the length measurement (1); (ii) Explain one precaution for accurate measurements (2).
items.ms: (i) %U = 0.1 mm / 20 mm x 100 = 0.5%. (ii) Any one precaution with its reason: repeat readings and average to minimise random error; measure at several places on the tile and average to allow for variation in dimensions; or check for zero error on the vernier/micrometer to correct systematic error.

items.name: Mean tile volume and its uncertainty
items.how: (i) Determine the mean volume of the tile from tabulated repeat readings of length (23.4 mm), width (23.1 mm) and thickness (7.93 to 7.97 mm) (2); the mark scheme also has (ii) the percentage uncertainty in the volume (3), not in the extracted text.
items.ms: (i) Mean volume = 23.4 x 23.1 x 7.95 = 4297 mm^3, given as 4.30 x 10^-6 m^3 to 3 s.f. with unit (second mark depends on the first). (ii) Half-range for each quantity (0.2, 0.1, 0.02 mm), %U each (0.85%, 0.43%, 0.25%), add them to give about 1.5%.

items.name: Glass density and comparison with crown glass
items.how: (i) Calculate the density of the glass from mass 10.03 g (negligible uncertainty) and the mean volume (2); the mark scheme also has (ii) deciding whether the tile is crown glass (2500 kg m^-3) by comparison with the uncertainty (2), not in the extracted text.
items.ms: (i) Use density = m/V; 10.03 x 10^-3 kg / 4.30 x 10^-6 m^3 = 2330 kg m^-3 to 3 s.f. with unit (ecf from 1(b)(i)). (ii) Calculate upper/lower limit using the %U (about 2360 kg m^-3) and compare with 2500, or compare the percentage difference (6.8%) with the %U; conclude the tile is probably not crown glass.

deps.name: Mean tile volume and its uncertainty

items.name: Why thermistor resistance falls with temperature
items.how: State why the resistance of a thermistor decreases as its temperature increases (context: current through a thermistor between 0 and 100 deg C).
items.ms: A greater number of conduction (free) electrons/charge carriers at higher temperature (1 mark).

items.name: Constant p.d. and thermistor circuit diagram
items.how: Student keeps the p.d. across the thermistor constant: (i) State why this is important (1); (ii) Draw a circuit diagram for the investigation (3).
items.ms: (i) So that p.d. does not affect the current, i.e. only temperature affects the current. (ii) Power supply and thermistor (1), a means of adjusting the p.d. such as variable supply or variable resistor (1), ammeter and voltmeter in the correct positions (1).

items.name: Apparatus and technique for thermistor temperature control
items.how: (i) List the additional apparatus needed to change and measure the thermistor temperature from 0 to 100 deg C (2); (ii) Suggest one technique (question wording truncated in the extracted text) to improve the temperature measurement (1).
items.ms: (i) Beaker of water/ice and a thermometer (1); ice and a heater for the water (1). (ii) Any one: remove the heater just before taking a reading, place the thermometer and thermistor close together, or stir the water.

items.name: Small amplitude for spring oscillations
items.how: State why a small amplitude of oscillation should be used each time when timing a mass on a spring with T = 2 pi sqrt(m/k).
items.ms: So the system performs simple harmonic motion (1 mark).

items.name: Accurate measurement of oscillation period
items.how: Describe how the student can make sure that the value of T, timed with a stopwatch, is as accurate as possible.
items.ms: Time n oscillations and divide by n (1); use a fiducial marker at the centre of the oscillation, or repeat and calculate a mean (1).

items.name: Linearising T-m data and finding rock mass
items.how: (i) Explain which graph to plot to obtain a straight line from readings of m and T (2); (ii) State how to determine the mass of the rock from the graph (1).
items.ms: (i) Plot T^2 against m (T^2 = 4 pi^2 m / k is y = mx), or T against sqrt(m), or log T against log m, with the reason that it is of the form y = mx (+ c). (ii) Measure T for the rock, then read m from the graph (calculating T^2 or log T as needed to be consistent with the graph in (i)).

items.name: Data logger versus stopwatch for period
items.how: Suggest how a position sensor and data logger, rather than a stopwatch, would improve the accuracy of the spring-oscillation experiment.
items.ms: Eliminates human reaction time, or allows the time to be read at an exact position (1 mark).

items.name: Accurate capacitor discharge measurements
items.how: State two additional ways the technician could make her capacitor-discharge measurements of V and t as accurate as possible (repeats and mean values already used).
items.ms: One from: use the same initial p.d., charge the capacitor fully, or check the voltmeter for zero error (1). One from: place voltmeter close to stopwatch so both are read together, use the lap timer, or use a data logger so V and t are measured simultaneously (1).

items.name: Why ln V against t is linear
items.how: Explain why a graph of ln V against t is a straight line for V = V0 e^(-t/RC).
items.ms: Take logs: ln V = ln V0 - t/RC, which is of the form y = c + mx (1); the gradient -1/RC is constant (1).

items.name: ln V against t graph and capacitance
items.how: Given a table of mean V against t (0 to 60 s, V from 6.00 V to 2.59 V) and R = 68 kilohm: (i) Draw a graph of ln V against t, adding a processed-data column (6); (ii) Use the graph to determine C (3).
items.ms: (i) ln(V/V) values correct to 3 or 4 s.f. (1.792 to 0.952), suitable scales using over half the grid, axes labelled ln(V/V) and t/s, accurate plots (2 marks), best-fit line (1). (ii) Gradient from a large triangle (about -0.0141 per s), use gradient = -1/RC (RC about 70.9 s), then C = 70.9 / 68 x 10^3 = 1.04 x 10^-3 F to 3 s.f. with unit.

deps.name: Why ln V against t is linear

items.name: Mean rolling time and percentage uncertainty
items.how: Five repeat times (2.37, 2.33, 2.36, 2.29, 2.32 s) for a marble rolling down a ramp: (i) Calculate the mean t (1); (ii) Calculate the percentage uncertainty in t (2).
items.ms: (i) Mean t = 2.33 s. (ii) Use half the range (0.04 s) (1) and %U = 0.04 / 2.33 x 100 = 1.7% (1); if the whole range is used only the second mark is available.

items.name: Height uncertainty, g calculation and evaluation
items.how: Student records the change in height as 3.4 cm +/- 0.2 cm using a metre rule and set square: (i) Explain why the uncertainty is +/- 0.2 cm (2); the mark scheme also has (ii) calculate g (1), (iii) the percentage uncertainty in g (3) and (iv) whether the value of g is accurate (2), which are not in the extracted question text.
items.ms: (i) Rule resolution is 1 mm (1); two heights are subtracted, so their absolute uncertainties add (1). (ii) g = 9.7 m s^-2 using mean t = 2.33 s, s = 0.800 m and 3.4 cm. (iii) %U in s (0.125%) and in delta h (5.88%), double the %U in t, add to give 9.6% (10% accepted). (iv) Compute upper/lower limit (about 10.6 m s^-2) and note the accepted g lies within it, or compare %D (1.1%) with %U; value is accurate.

deps.name: Mean rolling time and percentage uncertainty

items.name: Light gates versus stopwatch for accuracy
items.how: Discuss whether using light gates to time the marble rolling to the finish line would improve the accuracy of the value of g.
items.ms: Max 2 from: light gates remove human reaction time (1), so the %U in t falls (1, dependent); or gates are awkward with small objects/not measuring from centre of mass (1); %U in delta h is more significant, so the overall improvement is small (1).

deps.name: Height uncertainty, g calculation and evaluation

items.name: Instrument for lead sheet thickness
items.how: Explain which measuring instrument should be used to measure the thickness of each of 16 lead sheets of approximately 1 mm.
items.ms: Micrometer screw gauge, or digital calipers with 0.01 mm resolution (1); percentage uncertainty is about 1%, which is small (1).

items.name: Variables to control in gamma absorption
items.how: State any variables the student should control when investigating absorption of gamma radiation by lead.
items.ms: The distance between the source and the Geiger-Muller tube (1 mark).

items.name: Accurate count rate measurement
items.how: Describe how the student should make sure the recorded count rate is accurate.
items.ms: Subtract the background count (rate) from the measured count (rate) (1); record counts over a long time, or repeat and calculate a mean (1).

items.name: Radioactive source safety precaution
items.how: State one safety precaution when using a radioactive source.
items.ms: Any one: minimise time of use, store in a lead-lined box, do not point the source at the body, handle with forceps/tongs. Protective clothing or goggles are not accepted.

items.name: Show capacitor energy results fit W = 1/2 CV^2
items.how: Show that results (V = 6.0, 4.5, 3.0 V with W = 8.47, 4.76, 2.11 mJ) are consistent with W = 1/2 CV^2.
items.ms: Rearrange to C = 2W/V^2 (or state W/V^2 is constant) (1); calculate C for all three readings (about 4.7 x 10^-4 F each) (1); comment that the constant values are consistent with the equation (1).

items.name: Time constant meaning and voltmeter resistance
items.how: Capacitor charged to 6.0 V and discharged through an analogue voltmeter, with a V against t graph: (i) State the significance of the time constant (1); (ii) Determine the resistance R of the voltmeter (2).
items.ms: (i) Time for charge or p.d. to fall to 1/e (37%) of its initial value, or to fall by 63%. (ii) Use the graph to find the time constant (or half-life) (1); R = tau / C = 95 s / 4.7 x 10^-4 F, about 200 kilohm (1), ecf from 3(a).

deps.name: Show capacitor energy results fit W = 1/2 CV^2

items.name: Accurate period measurement for oscillating mass
items.how: Student's plan: marker at equilibrium, time at least 10 oscillations and divide, repeat and take a mean. Explain how this method ensures that the period T is as accurate as possible.
items.ms: Marker at equilibrium gives a more accurate start/end of oscillation (1); timing multiple oscillations reduces the percentage uncertainty (1); repeating and averaging reduces the effect of random errors (1).

items.name: Why log T against log M is linear
items.how: For T = q M^r, explain why plotting log T against log M should produce a straight-line graph.
items.ms: log T = r log M + log q is of the form y = mx + c (1); the gradient r is constant (1).

items.name: Plot log-log graph and find q and r
items.how: Given six pairs of M (0.300 to 0.800 kg) and T (0.416 to 0.664 s): (i) Plot log T against log M, using additional columns for processed data (6); (ii) Determine the constants q and r and hence state the relationship between T and M (4).
items.ms: (i) log M and log T correct to 3 or 4 s.f. (ln labelled as ln if used), axes labelled log(M/kg) and log(T/s), suitable scales over half the grid, accurate plots, best-fit line drawn to x = 0 (6). (ii) Gradient from a large triangle gives r (about 0.46, positive, no unit), intercept gives q (about 0.72), then state T = 0.72 M^0.46 (4).

deps.name: Why log T against log M is linear

items.name: Folded sheet thickness: reason and technique
items.how: A thin metal sheet (sides 30.0 +/- 0.1 cm) folded in half five times and measured with a micrometer: (i) State one reason for measuring the folded sheet rather than an unfolded sheet (1); (ii) Explain one other technique for an accurate thickness measurement (2).
items.ms: (i) A larger thickness reduces the percentage uncertainty (not just 'uncertainty'). (ii) Any one technique with its reason (second mark depends on the first): repeat at different places and average to reduce random errors; check micrometer zero error to remove systematic error; use the ratchet to avoid squashing the metal; squeeze out air gaps; or measure away from the fold edge as the fold is thicker.

items.name: Micrometer readings, mean thickness and uncertainty
items.how: From pictured micrometer scale readings: (i) Record the measurements in a table of total thickness (2); (ii) Calculate the mean thickness and the corresponding uncertainty (2).
items.ms: (i) Values consistent with mm units, listed as 0.47, 0.49, 0.47, 0.48 (2 s.f., any order). (ii) Mean = 0.48 mm to 2 s.f. (1); absolute uncertainty from half the range = 0.01 mm (1); ecf from (i) for both.

items.name: Metal density from folded sheet, identification
items.how: Folded sheet has mass 3.62 +/- 0.01 g: (i) Calculate a value for the density in kg m^-3 (2); the mark scheme also has (ii) a conclusion about which metal it could be, using the percentage uncertainty (3), not in the extracted question text.
items.ms: (i) Use rho = m/V with V = 0.30 x 0.30 x (0.48 x 10^-3)/32 (five folds give 32 layers), giving about 2680 kg m^-3 (2700 accepted), ecf from (b)(ii). (ii) %U = 2 x 0.1/30 + 0.01/0.48 + 0.01/3.62 = 3.1%; upper limit about 2780 kg m^-3, or %D = 0.37% compared with %U; the quoted density falls within the limits so the metal could be aluminium.

deps.name: Micrometer readings, mean thickness and uncertainty

items.name: Cooling curve gradient and heat loss rate
items.how: Graph of temperature of 100 cm^3 of hot water against time: (i) Determine the gradient of the graph at 70.0 deg C (2); (ii) Hence calculate the rate of thermal energy transfer to the surroundings, given density and specific heat capacity (2). The mark scheme also shows a part (b) (5 marks, not in the extracted text): a variable to control, how to compare cooling rates, and why repeats are difficult.
items.ms: (i) Tangent drawn at 70.0 deg C and gradient from it in the range -2.80 to -3.10 deg C per minute (example -2.93). (ii) Use dE/dt = m c dtheta/dt: 100 g x 4.2 J per g K x 2.93 = about 1230 J per min (20 to 22 W), ecf. Part (b): control volume/mass, surroundings temperature or initial temperature; compare gradients at the same temperature (or time for same temperature change); surroundings temperature is hard to keep constant so repeats are not appropriate.

items.name: Meaning of damping
items.how: State what is meant by damping, in the context of a vertical mass-spring system with a cardboard disc.
items.ms: Energy is (permanently) removed/dissipated from the system (1), resulting in a decrease in amplitude (1).

items.name: Why ln A against n gives decay constant
items.how: For A = A0 e^(-lambda n), explain why a graph of ln A against n can be used to determine lambda.
items.ms: ln A = ln A0 - lambda n (1), which is of the form y = c + mx with constant gradient -lambda (1); second mark dependent on the first.

items.name: ln A against n graph and decay constant
items.how: Mean amplitudes A (13.8 to 10.3 cm) for oscillations 1 to 6 are given: (i) Plot ln A against n with a processed-data column (5); (ii) Use your graph to determine lambda (2).
items.ms: (i) ln A correct to 3 or 4 s.f., axes ln(A/cm) and n, suitable scales, plots within 1 mm, line of best fit. (ii) Gradient from a large triangle (1); lambda to 2 or 3 s.f., positive, no unit (1).

deps.name: Why ln A against n gives decay constant

items.name: Data logger improving amplitude accuracy
items.how: The experiment is modified to use a data logger and position sensor. Explain how this may lead to a more accurate value for A.
items.ms: High sampling rate near the maximum displacement (1); parallax error at the maximum displacement is eliminated (1).

items.name: Bar magnets force apparatus and method + Verifying power-law force-distance relationship
items.how: Describe how the data collected in (a) should be used to verify F = a x^b (marked holistically with part a).
items.ms: Multiply balance readings by g to obtain F, or state the readings are proportional to F (1); plot log F against log x (or ln F against ln x) (1); check it is a straight line / has a constant gradient (1).

items.name: Vernier calipers: coin diameter and stack thickness
items.how: Density of coin metal with 20 identical coins and vernier calipers: (i) Describe how to accurately determine the diameter d of a coin (2); (ii) wording truncated in the extracted text, but the mark scheme shows it asks why measuring a stack of 20 coins for thickness (about 2 mm each) is better (3).
items.ms: (i) Check for zero error (1); repeat at different orientations and calculate a mean (1). (ii) A larger stack reduces the percentage uncertainty (1) because the uncertainty (calipers resolution 0.1 mm) is the same in both measurements (1); single coin about 5% against 0.25% for 20 coins (1).

items.name: Coin density, uncertainty and cupronickel comparison
items.how: Given d = 2.24 cm, 20t = 5.76 cm and mass of 20 coins 190.4 g: (i) Determine the density in g cm^-3 (2); (ii) State why the percentage uncertainty in d should be small (1); the mark scheme also has (iii) (4 marks, not in the extracted text) on the percentage uncertainty in density and comparing with a quoted density.
items.ms: (i) Use rho = m/V with V = pi (d/2)^2 x (20t), giving 8.39 g cm^-3. (ii) d is squared so its percentage uncertainty is doubled. (iii) %U in d (0.45%) and t (0.52%) give %U in rho = 1.4%; compare 8.39 with the upper limit (8.51), or %D (5.3%) with %U; the quoted 8.86 g cm^-3 for cupronickel is outside, so the coin is not cupronickel.

items.name: Laser safety precaution
items.how: State one safety precaution when using a laser (context: measuring a hair diameter by diffraction).
items.ms: Any one: avoid looking directly into the laser beam, or avoid reflective surfaces.

items.name: Minima from two coherent sources of light
items.how: Light diffracts from each side of a hair and acts as two coherent sources, giving an interference pattern on a screen. Explain how positions of minimum intensity are formed.
items.ms: The two coherent waves arrive out of phase (1) and destructive interference occurs (1).

items.name: Effect of doubling D on percentage uncertainty
items.how: For d = lambda D / s (lambda wavelength, D hair-to-screen distance, s distance between consecutive minima), explain the effect of doubling D on the percentage uncertainty in d.
items.ms: Doubling D halves its own percentage uncertainty (1); with D and lambda constant, s also doubles and its percentage uncertainty also halves (1); hence the percentage uncertainty in d is halved (1).

items.name: Measurements to test power-flux relationship
items.how: Filament bulb luminosity: radiation flux F is measured by a sensor at a fixed distance and P = kF^4 is suggested. Describe the measurements that should be made to test the relationship.
items.ms: Measure the p.d. and current (1), with corresponding values of light intensity (flux) (1); marked holistically with parts b and c.

items.name: Circuit diagram for filament bulb
items.how: Draw a circuit diagram to show how the filament bulb should be connected for measuring power input.
items.ms: Power supply, bulb and a means of varying the current (1); voltmeter and ammeter connected correctly (1).

items.name: Testing validity of P = kF^4
items.how: Explain how the measurements will be used to test the validity of P = kF^4.
items.ms: Calculate P = IV (1); plot P against F^4 (1), which is of the form y = mx (+ c) (1), giving a straight line through the origin with gradient k if valid (1). Alternative: plot log P against log F, log P = 4 log F + log k, expecting a straight line of gradient 4.

deps.name: Measurements to test power-flux relationship

items.name: Accurate thermistor temperature measurement techniques
items.how: Thermistor in a cooling beaker of hot water, resistance read by ohmmeter and temperature by thermometer: State two techniques to make the measurement of temperature as accurate as possible.
items.ms: Any two: stir the water, keep the thermometer close to the thermistor, allow the water to cool slowly.

items.name: ln R against theta graph, alpha and series resistor
items.how: For R = R0 e^(-alpha theta) with seven (theta, R) pairs from 80 deg C to 0 deg C: (i) Plot ln R against theta with a processed-data column (5); (ii) Use the graph to determine alpha (4); the mark scheme also has (iii) (3 marks, not in the extracted text) using R = V/I to find a series resistor value.
items.ms: (i) ln R correct to 3 or 4 s.f. (-0.470 to 2.573), axes ln(R/kilohm) and theta/deg C, suitable scales, plots within 1 mm, best-fit line.
